->**In the Name of Jesus**<-
<note>original: "I. N. J." — abbreviation for "In Nomine Jesu," a common pious invocation at the start of scholarly works in the early modern period.</note>

It is well known to everyone, and has been proven by more than one example, that the extent of errors is so vast that they occupy the minds of all and force them, as it were, under their own laws. Even the pagans <term>gentiles: a term used here to refer to non-Christian classical thinkers, such as the Greeks and Romans</term> could not be brought to deny this; indeed, they erred more excusably because they proved themselves to be more open and ready witnesses and critics of their own mistakes. Regarding this matter, the work of **THOMAS GATAKER** <note>A 17th-century English scholar known for his commentary on Marcus Aurelius.</note> deserves to be read *on Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, Book V, § 22 and Book II, § 1*; as does the work of **TOBIAS PFANNER** in his *System of Gentile Theology, Chapter IX, § 7.*

Hence, even those who labor with the greatest mental effort to repel errors are not themselves immune from the danger of erring. This was demonstrated not only by **FRANÇOIS DE LA MOTHE LE VAYER** <note>A French skeptic philosopher.</note> and others in the *Rustic Hexameron* <note>original: "Hexaëmero Rustico" — a work discussing various scholarly errors and perspectives</note>, *page 18 and following*, where he brought to light the "hallucinations" <term>allucinationibus: in this context, it refers to intellectual lapses, oversights, or errors in judgment made by even the most brilliant scholars</term> of the most excellent men. Furthermore, proof is provided by the examples of those who have corrected their own errors. A bountiful harvest of such examples, from both ancient and more recent times, has been provided to the Most Reverend **CASPAR NEUMANN**, my Patron and Teacher—

...to the excellent author, in his most elegant discourse on the **Retractions of the Fathers**, reprinted with his **Academic First Fruits**, page 112 and following; likewise to **Johann Schmid** in his *Dissertation on the Recantations of the Learned*, Leipzig, 1697; to **Paganino Gaudenzi** <note>An Italian polymath and professor known for his vast reading and critique of literature.</note> in *The Midwife of Literature, Dissertation X*, page 86 and following; and to **Almeloveen** <note>Theodoor Jansson van Almeloveen, a Dutch physician and classical scholar.</note> on page 97 of his work *On New-Ancient Inventions*.

Just as this commonality of erring should seem surprising to no one who has seen the source and spring of common error; so too, I believe, it will seem a wondrous thing to many that such errors exist which have touched the minds of almost everyone, and, having been received by the consensus of nearly everyone, have taken on no small appearance of truth. 

Indeed, certain wise men, who were engaged in collecting errors of this kind, have ensured that we doubt this less. Specifically, **Thomas Browne**, the famous English physician—whom **Lipenius** in the *Philosophical Library*, page 474b, and **König** in the *Library of the Old and New*, page 139, confused with his namesake <note>original: "ὁμωνύμῳ" (homōnymō) — the author is correcting a bibliographical error where the famous doctor Sir Thomas Browne was confused with Robert Browne, the founder of the "Brownist" religious sect.</note>, the leader of the Brownist sect—in his *Inquiries into Common Errors* <note>original: "Inquisitionibus in vulgi errores" — referring to the Latin edition of Browne's famous 1646 work, *Pseudodoxia Epidemica*.</note>, and **Laurent Joubert** in his book written in French *On Popular Errors*, about which the distinguished **Pierre Bayle** <note>Author of the influential "Historical and Critical Dictionary," a cornerstone of early Enlightenment thought.</note> deserves to be read in Volume II of his *Historical-Critical Dictionary*, page 1654.

...of them <note>The author is continuing a sentence describing systems of error; specifically, those regarding the nature of God and the universe.</note>, one makes God the **material cause** of all things and asserts that all things have emanated from the divine essence as if from a **most fertile fountain**; the other, not very different, divides the divine sovereignty and invents various principles to which the whole framework of things owes its formation. The former view was so approved by the gentiles that for a long time learned men have seen the whole mass of **Paganism** as built upon it as a foundation. 

Read, if you please, **Cudworth** <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), a leading figure among the Cambridge Platonists.</note>, the most learned of English writers, in his *Intellectual System of this Universe*, written in English <note>original: "System. Regarding the **Creation** of this universe, the **Gentile** <note>Meaning non-Christian or pagan philosophers of antiquity.</note> philosophers go in different directions and are divided into three main branches. It cannot be denied that the origin of matter was attributed to God as its author by the most ancient philosophers of the nations, whatever **Burnet** <note>Thomas Burnet (c. 1635–1715), an English theologian famous for his *Sacred Theory of the Earth*. original: "BURNETUS"</note> might bring to the contrary in his

The Gentile himself <note>Referring to the Roman Stoic philosopher Seneca, mentioned on the previous page.</note> says in Epistle 95: *“These [the Gods], he believes, neither grant evil nor possess it; however, they do chastise and restrain, and they impose penalties, and sometimes punish under the appearance of evil.”* Yet this same philosopher—to hide nothing—did not sufficiently guard himself against a vice common among the Stoics: the stain of contradiction. Anyone who compares the quoted words of Seneca with his own writings in Book 2 of *On Anger*, chapter 27, and Book 6 of *Natural Questions*, chapter 3, and other passages, will sense that he is infected by it. In those works, he confidently pronounces the Gods to be free from all anger or the desire to punish human beings, failing to remember his own words, as **BAYLE** <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a famous French philosopher and skeptic.</note> demonstrates in his *Continuation of Miscellaneous Thoughts on the Comet*, section 61, page 301 and following. 

From this, the gentiles further believed that even evils are so governed by God that they turn toward a good end and conspire completely toward the preservation of this universe. The same may be read in **GATAKER** <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), an English scholar known for his commentary on Marcus Aurelius.</note> on page 54, regarding Book 6, section 42. They applied such great effort to free God, the source of all goodness, from the impure filth of sin! 

Yet from there, they turned to the other extreme by joining an evil principle to this good one, and in doing so, they fabricated the origin of evil rather than truly explaining it. And by this reasoning, we find the origin of the error concerning two contrary principles <note>This refers to dualism, the belief that there are two equal and opposite powers—one good and one evil—governing the world.</note> in this double cause that pushes the minds of men toward accepting it. **PLUTARCH** <note>A Greek historian and philosopher (c. 46–119 AD).</note> summarized this in his work *On Isis and Osiris*, page 369, with these words: "For if nothing is naturally born without a cause, and a good thing cannot provide the cause for evil, it must..." <note>original Greek: "Εἰ γὰρ οὐδὲν ἀναιτίως πέφυκε γενέσθαι, αἰτίαν δὲ κακοῦ ἀγαθὸν οὐκ ἂν παράσχοι, δεῖ..." The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 45. While the previous page (44) concluded with a discussion on the corruption of Jewish philosophy, this page shifts to a philological and historical investigation into the origins of the "Chaldeans" and how their name was used by ancient authors.</meta>

...the most ancient class of Teachers, as **Cicero** calls them in *On Divination*, book I. <note>Cicero identifies the Chaldeans not just as a people, but as a specific caste of learned men.</note> By this name [Chaldeans], those among the Babylonians and Assyrians were first called—according to the witness of **Diogenes Laertius** in section 1 of his *Proem*—who devoted themselves to wisdom and took care of sacred things; so that at the beginning it was the name of a sect, which in succeeding time came to denote an entire people. Compare **Diodorus Siculus**, book II, p. 81 D and p. 78 C, where he says: "the Babylonians call the priests Chaldeans" <note>original Greek: ἱερέας Βαβυλώνιοι καλέσι χαλδαίες</note>. Add to this **Clement of Alexandria**, book I, p. 305. 

An even broader change happened to the meaning of this word: while at first it was restricted to the Babylonian people alone, later, by Eastern writers of a more recent age—and especially by the Arabs—not only they but also the Nabataeans, Canaanites, and Sabaeans were marked by the name of *Chasdim* or *Chaldanim* <note>These are the Hebrew and Aramaic forms of "Chaldeans," often used in the Bible and later Rabbinic literature.</note>, as noted by **Thomas Stanley** in *History of Oriental Philosophy*, book III, p. 344. XII. Having settled these matters, some points must still be brought forward regarding the naming of both Principles. From what has been established above, it is clear that the Good principle was called **Oromasdes**, and the evil one **Arimanius**. Many have investigated the reasoning behind these names, which **Plutarch** <note>Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD) was a Greek philosopher and biographer whose work *On Isis and Osiris* is a major source for ancient Persian religion.</note> expressed quite clearly on page 369 of *On Isis and Osiris*: "This man (Zoroaster)," he says, "called the one Oromazes and the other Arimanius, and further declared that the former resembled light more than any other thing perceived by the senses, while the latter, on the contrary, resembled darkness and ignorance." <note>original Greek: "οὗτος οὖν (ζωροάστρης) ἐκάλει τὸν μὲν Ωρομάζην τὸν δὲ Αρειμάνιον, καὶ προσαπεφαίνετο, τὸν μὲν ἐοικέναι τῷ φωτὶ, μάλιστα τῶν αἰσθητῶν, τὸν δὲ ἔμπαλιν σκότῳ καὶ ἀγνοίᾳ."</note> He says that Zoroaster likened the Good principle to light, and the evil to darkness and ignorance. 

The names themselves suggest this very thing, as there is hardly anyone who would not derive *Oromasdes* from **Or** <note>Hebrew: אור (*or*), meaning light.</note> or "light," although writers differ greatly regarding the second part of the word. **Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a Swiss theologian and scholar.</note>, in his *Index to Stanley* <note>Referring to Thomas Stanley’s *History of Philosophy*.</note> under the entry *Oromasdes*, thinks that two words, **Or Amaya** <note>Aramaic/Hebrew: אור אמיא, translated here as "splendent fire."</note> (that is, "shining fire"), gave the name its origin. **Windet** <note>James Windet (d. 1664), an English physician and scholar.</note>, however, on page 36 of *On the State of the Departed*, derives it from **Or** ("light" or "fire") and **Mazar** <note>Hebrew: מצר (*mazar*), meaning "he guarded" or "fortified."</note> (meaning "he guarded" or "fortified"). **Hyde** <note>Thomas Hyde, the orientalist mentioned on the previous page.</note> repeats this same idea in Chapter IX, page 161, and brings forward an etymology <term>etymology: the study of the origin of words</term> which suggests that supplication should be made under the name of Oromasdes. Finally, **Kipping** <note>Heinrich Kipping (1623–1678), a German historian and philologist.</note> in *Roman Antiquities*, Book I, Chapter VI, Section II, page 163, derives it from **Or** and **Shamar** <note>Hebrew: שמר (*shamar*), which Kipping here interprets as "he destroyed."</note> (meaning "he destroyed"), though, in my opinion, this is less fitting.

For where the words have been read thus far as, "Zoroaster introduces one as the leader of all, whom he also calls Fortune," <note>original Greek: ἓν καὶ ἀρχηγὸν πάντων εἰσάγει ζαράσδης ὃν καὶ τύχην καλεῖ</note> Tollius prefers to read, "whom he also calls a beam of light," <note>original Greek: ὃν καὶ αὐγὴν καλεῖ</note> because the good God would take his name from light.

Now the same labor must be performed for **Arimanius**, whose name has been subject to various conjectures. **Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736) was a Swiss theologian and scholar.</note> indeed thinks it is derived from *ari* (ערי), that is, "enemy," and *mad* (מאד), that is, "vessel," which he believes can be taken metaphorically for a person or a person's body. One might also derive it, with the same author's approval, from the Egyptian *arum* (ערום), that is, "shrewd" or "crafty," since that name reflects it exactly if it is pronounced *Arimon* with an additional syllable in the Arabic fashion. **Windet** <note>James Windet (d. 1664) was an English physician and scholar of ancient religions.</note> in the passage previously cited traces it back to *aram* (ערם), using these words: "Arimanius seems to have been named from *aram*, which signifies 'to heap up' or 'accumulate' in both the Hebrew and Chaldean languages,"

XIII. **Plutarch** <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 119 AD) was a Greek philosopher and biographer; his work *On Isis and Osiris* is a major source for ancient Middle Eastern religions.</note> in his work *On Isis and Osiris* is the authority for the fact that the worship of both deities <note>referring to the principles of Light/Good and Darkness/Evil</note> was highly commended to the Persians; indeed, it would be a sin to doubt the veneration of **Oromasdis** <note>The Greek form of Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of Zoroastrianism.</note>. For it has been well established that the Persians exhibited great honor toward fire, which they transferred especially to the sun, as if it were the sun’s primary receptacle. From this, they held fire as sacred—see **Hyde** <note>Thomas Hyde, *History of the Religion of the Ancient Persians*, Chapter 1.</note>, Chapter I—and in various places they constructed *fire-temples* <note>original Greek: πυρεῖα ("pyreia"), structures specifically for housing a sacred flame</note>, in which a perpetual fire was nourished, much like that of the Jews, according to the same author in Chapter VIII. The worship of the Sun among them is no less certain and proven; indeed, the most ancient writers of Greece clearly saw that they worshipped the sun under the name of *Mithra*. For **Strabo** <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) was a Greek geographer.</note> testifies that *Mithra* is the sun in the 15th book of his *Geography*, page 503: "They honor," he says of the Persians, "the sun, whom they call Mithra" <note>original Greek: Τιμῶσι δὲ... τὸν ἥλιον, ὃν καλοῦσι, Μίθραν.</note>. Likewise, **Hesychius** <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer.</note> states: "Mithras, the sun among the Persians" <note>original Greek: Μίθρας, ὁ ἥλιος παρὰ πέρσαις.</note>. See more passages in the work of the most learned **Gataker** <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), an English scholar and theologian.</note> in *Critical Works*, Chapter XXI, *Miscellaneous Adversaria*, page 659 and following; **Vossius** <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, Book II, Chapter IX, page 350; **Halloix** <note>Pierre Halloix (1571–1656), a Jesuit hagiographer.</note> in the *Life of Justin*, page 256 and following; **Grabe** <note>John Ernest Grabe (1666–1711), an Anglican divine and scholar.</note> in Volume I of the *Spicilegium of the Fathers of the Second Century*, page 240, and in his notes on *Justin Martyr’s First Apology*, where **Vossius'** *On Idolatry*, Book IX, is cited—perhaps by a typographical error, since Book II ought to have been cited.

Great weight is added to this opinion concerning the sun, worshipped under the name of Mithra, by the etymology of the name, which **Hyde** <note>*On the Religion of the Ancient Persians*, Chapter IV.</note> thinks is an epithet for the Sun, deriving it from the Persian *Mihr*...

...which carries the meaning of love and mercy. **Scaliger** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609) was a foundational figure in the study of historical chronology.</note> however, saw it differently in *Book VI of On the Emendation of Time*, in the chapter regarding the week. **Plutarch** must have preferred another etymology, since on page 369 of the book cited above, he says of Zoroaster: <note>original Greek: Ἐκάλει τὸν μὲν Ὡρομάζην τὸν δὲ Ἀρειμάνεον· μέσον δὲ ἀμφοῖν τὸν Μίθρην εἶναι διὸ καὶ Μίθρην Πέρσαι τὸν μεσίτην ὀνομάζουσι.</note> "He called the one **Oromazes** <note>Ahura Mazda, the principle of Light</note> and the other **Arimanius** <note>Ahriman, the principle of Darkness</note>; and **Mithras** is in the middle of both, which is why the Persians call Mithras the *Mediator*." 

This anxious concern for the worship of Fire and the Sun gave the Persians the reputation of being idolaters and "fire-worshippers" among many, since the opinion prevailed that the Persians counted the Sun just as much as fire among the number of their Gods. This is the position held by almost all the authors cited above, to whom you may add **Filippo della Torre** <note>Filippo della Torre (1657–1717) was an Italian antiquarian and bishop known for his studies of ancient monuments.</note> in his *Fourth Dissertation*, which is attached to the *Monuments of Ancient Antium*; compare also Bernhard's *New Literary Republic*, page 374 and following, and the *Memoirs of Trévoux*, Volume V, 1703, page 788. 

Della Torre elegantly observes that the Persians celebrated the birthday of Mithras with a solemn rite, perhaps for the reason that the Sun at that time <note>likely referring to the Winter Solstice</note> seems, as it were, to be reborn and to resume new strength. 

However, more insightful scholars hold an entirely different view. They are convinced that the Persians practiced a symbolic worship of fire and the sun, which they nevertheless intended to be directed toward God Himself—that is, the Principle of Good. **Hyde** <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703) was a pioneering English Orientalist who argued that the ancient Persians were actually monotheists.</note> fought for this opinion especially in Chapters I and IV of his work. In the former section, on page 5, he says: "although they showed to it [meaning fire] a certain reverence,"

If we listen to *Plutarch in his work On Isis and Osiris*, the matter will be settled immediately. For he argues according to their <note>the Egyptians'</note> mind in this way, on pages 373 and following:

> <note>original Greek: "ἡ κρείττων καὶ θειοτέρα φύσις ἐκ τριῶν ἐστι, τοῦ Νοητοῦ καὶ τῆς ὕλης, καὶ τοῦ ἐκ τούτων, ὃν κόσμον Ἕλληνες ὀνομάζουσιν..."</note> *The more excellent and divine nature consists of three things: that which is perceived by the mind, matter, and that which is composed of these, which the Greeks call the world. Indeed, Plato is accustomed to call the first—the <term>Intelligible</term> <note>The realm of pure ideas or forms that can only be understood by the intellect, not the senses.</note>, the idea, and the exemplar—the **Father**; matter he calls the **Mother**, the **Nurse**, and the seat and region capable of receiving births; and that which consists of both he is accustomed to call the **offspring** and the **birth**.*

Later, he compares these three things to a triangle on page 374. *It must be understood,* he says, *that with one line standing at a right angle to the other, the male is represented; with the base stretching underneath, the female; and the offspring of both is represented [by the hypotenuse]: and Osiris is the principle, Isis the receptacle, and the birth is the result.* <note>Plutarch is describing the "Egyptian Triangle" (a 3-4-5 right triangle), where the vertical side (3) represents Osiris, the horizontal base (4) represents Isis, and the hypotenuse (5) represents their son Horus, symbolizing the harmony of the universe.</note>

Indeed, I am not unaware that there is a great controversy and disagreement of minds among the learned regarding this point of Egyptian doctrine. Even the Egyptian philosophers themselves—who understood Osiris to be the Moon or the Nile, Typhon to be both the Sun and the Sea, and Isis to be both the Moon and the Earth, as appears from the cited book of Plutarch—[disagreed]. **VOSSIUS** <note>Gerardus Joannes Vossius (1577–1649), a highly influential Dutch scholar of classical history and theology.</note> promises that he will explain this more accurately on page 35 of his book *On the Worship of Corporeal Nature* <note>original Latin: *de naturae corporeae cultu*</note> in his work *On Idolatry* <note>original: *de Idolol.* Referring to his 1641 work *De theologia gentili et physiologia christiana; sive De origine ac progressu idololatriae*.</note>.

The Phoenicians <note>original: Φοῖνιξες</note> draw a circular, airy, and fiery orb, and across the middle, they stretch a hawk-shaped serpent. The entire figure is shaped like our letter **Theta** (Θ). By the circle, they indicate the world; and by the serpent in the middle, they signify the "Good Spirit" <note>original: ἀγαθὸν δαίμονα (*agathon daimona*), a benevolent protector spirit in Greek and Egyptian thought</note> that holds the universe together.

By this same token, they represent the world through the Circle, and by the Serpent in the middle—joining it from both sides—they signify that same Good Spirit.

I would not deny that many writers, here and elsewhere, have "dreamed" that the Egyptians possessed a knowledge of the **Trinity**, but they are equipped with arguments that are equally weak—that is to say, invalid. Thus **Malelas** <note>John Malalas (c. 491–578), a Byzantine chronicler.</note> in his *Chronographia*, pages 29 and following, brings forward several passages from the writings of **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure portrayed as an ancient Egyptian sage and author of the *Hermetica*.</note> cited by **Cyril** <note>Cyril of Alexandria, who often quoted Hermetic texts to prove pagan awareness of Christian truths.</note>, from which he thinks it is apparent: "that even Hermes Trismegistus, though ignorant of the future, confessed a **consubstantial Trinity**" <note>original: Τριάδα ὁμοούσιον (*Triada homoousion*). This term "consubstantial" is the central pillar of the Nicene Creed, used to describe the same essence of Father and Son.</note>. 

But I fear that unless that author knows how to make his opinion seem true using other testimonies and monuments, he will find few followers or "like-minded voters" <note>original: ὁμοψήφους (*homopsēphous*), those who cast the same vote.</note>. For those who truly understand these matters rightly grant very little faith to the writings of **Trismegistus**, seeing as they are partly fabricated and partly altered <note>By the 17th century, scholars like Isaac Casaubon had proven that the Hermetic writings were not ancient Egyptian but were written in the early centuries AD.</note>. See **Huet** in *Demonstration of the Gospel*, Proposition 4, chapter 4, section 2, page 128; **Cudworth** in *Intellectual System*, page 320; **Stillingfleet** in *Sacred Origins*, book 1, chapter 2, sections 9 and following, and pages 3 and 4 of the discourse added to the latest English edition of that book; and, he who is worth them all, the celebrated **Mr. Fabricius** in his exquisite work, *Greek Library*, book 1, chapter 7 and following. 

Furthermore, you may read more regarding this supposed Egyptian Trinity in **Cudworth**, page 313 and following, and...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 70, moving from a critique of the "Hermetic" Trinity to a Neoplatonic explanation of Egyptian polytheism. ### PETAVIUS *Theological Dogmas, Volume II, Book II, Chapter 2*

XV. Since these interpretations should be regarded as distortions rather than accurate accounts, I believe we should settle on the explanation that the authority of **Plutarch** <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer (c. 46–120 AD) who wrote *On Isis and Osiris*.</note> and **Philo of Byblos** <note>A writer (c. 64–141 AD) who claimed to translate ancient Phoenician religious texts.</note> has made most probable. Namely, the Egyptians established a single "Good Principle" which was addressed by various names. This is what **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who defended traditional Egyptian and Chaldean religion.</note> taught me in his work *On the Egyptian Mysteries*, when he says:

> The creative mind <note>original: ὁ δημιουργικὸς νῦς (*ho demiourgikos nous*)</note>, bringing the unseen power of hidden principles into the light, is called **Amun** in the language of the Egyptians; but when he accomplishes each thing truthfully and with craftsmanship, he is called **Phtha** <note>Ptah, the ancient Egyptian creator god associated with craftsmen and architects.</note>; and as the producer of good things, he is called **Osiris**; he also possesses other titles based on his various other powers and actions.

I believe these words should be expressed as follows: <note>The author provides a Latin translation of the Greek blockquote above, which is here rendered into English.</note> *The craftsman mind, bringing the obscure force of hidden words into the light, is called Amun in the Egyptian tongue; yet, completing all things without deception and skillfully, he is Phtha; while as the producer of good, he is called Osiris, and he holds other surnames due to other virtues and operations.* Anyone who has examined the customs of the pagans—who were in the habit of designating the same God with various names—will be easily persuaded of this. **Cudworth** <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), a Cambridge Platonist who argued that many ancient pagans were essentially monotheists.</note> proves this on pages 356 and following, and 488 and following of his *Intellectual System*, and he rightly judges that such a great abundance of gods flowed from this single source. Thus **Seneca** <note>The Roman Stoic philosopher (c. 4 BC – 65 AD).</note> says in *On Benefits*, Book I: *“You may assign whatever specific names you wish to Him, so long as they reflect some power and effect of heavenly matters.”* Likewise, **Zeno** <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note>, according to Laërtius <note>Diogenes Laërtius, a biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> in Book VII, 147, says: *“God is called by many titles.”*

<summary>The author argues that Egyptian polytheism was actually a form of monotheism where different gods like Amun, Ptah, and Osiris represented different attributes of a single "Creative Mind." He cites Neoplatonic and Stoic sources to support the idea that ancient pagans used multiple names for one divine essence.</summary>

He argues by a new reasoning that Osiris is called, as it were, *shur* <note>original Hebrew: שור</note>, that is, "ox," though he is beset by the same difficulty we noticed in **Le Clerc**.

### XVII. The Egyptian view of the Evil Principle

Having explained the opinion of the Egyptians regarding the Good principle, the plan of our undertaking requires that we also examine their antiquities concerning the Evil principle. For they join to **Osiris** a brother, **Typhon** <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, the deity of chaos, storms, and the desert.</note>, who is his greatest opposite and is inclined toward entirely contrary pursuits. Thus **PLUTARCH** <note>Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD), in his essay *On Isis and Osiris*.</note>, on page 351, in explaining his evil and hostile spirit toward Isis, says:

> "Isis is a Greek word <note>original: Ἑλληνικὸν... ἡ Ἶσις ἐστὶ. Plutarch mistakenly attempts to derive the Egyptian name Isis from the Greek verb "to know."</note>, and **Typhon** is an enemy to the goddess; through ignorance and deceit, he is puffed up <note>original Greek: τετυφωμένος (*tetuphomenos*). This is a pun on Typhon’s name and the Greek word *typhos*, meaning smoke, vanity, or a clouded mind.</note> and tears apart and does away with the sacred doctrine <note>original: τὸν ἱερὸν λόγον (*ton hieron logon*), or the "sacred word/reason."</note>, which the goddess collects, composes, and delivers to those being initiated for the attainment of divinity."

Regarding the battles fought by this same **Typhon** with **Horus** <note>The son of Osiris and Isis who eventually defeated Typhon to reclaim the throne of Egypt.</note>, from which Typhon finally emerged defeated, see the same author on page 358. To this medley of fables, Plutarch adds that they should not be regarded as empty fictions, such as poets and storytellers devise—who, like spiders, spin their beginnings out of themselves without any foundation—but rather that they contain within themselves certain philosophical discussions and accounts of actual events. This very same point is supported by the etymology of *Typhon* itself. [The author] is convinced that he was named from the Arabic *Tuban* <note>original: *Tuban*. Early modern scholars often looked to Arabic and Hebrew roots to explain Egyptian names, believing they shared a common "Oriental" origin.</note>, which designates a serpent, understanding this to refer to that ancient serpent <note>A common theological reference to the Devil or the serpent of Genesis.</note>. Nor is there any doubt that this reasoning for the name will find more approval among readers than the one provided by **PLUTARCH** from the Greek language, which is an origin entirely foreign to the subject. Others, however, have suggested different origins, and specifically those which they saw could best be recruited to support their own interpretations of the Egyptian myths.

Thus **BOCHART** <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant scholar famous for his works on Biblical geography and natural history.</note>, believing that **MOSES** was foreshadowed under the character of *Typhon*, strove to give his conjecture a certain appearance of truth by the reasoning of the name itself in his *Hierozoicon* <note>A massive 17th-century study of the animals mentioned in the Bible.</note>, *Book II, Chapter 34*. He thought **Typhon** was named from the Arabic *Tuphan*, which means *inundation* <note>original: *inundatio*. This refers to the Great Flood or a catastrophic overflowing of water.</note>, because **Moses** was the cause of the inundation of the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh’s army.

He was joined in this view by **HUET** in *Demonstratio Evangelica, page 346*; **WITSIUS**, who summarizes **Bochart’s** arguments in *Egyptiaca, Book III, Chapter IV, page 216 and following*; and **SCHUDT** in *Compendium of Jewish History, Chapter VII, page 57*. Nor are **CASALIUS**, in *On the Ancient Rites of the Egyptians, Chapter XXV, page 45*, and **Christoph Heinrich BROMEL**, in his *Dissertation on the Exterminating Angel, §. 31 and following*, far from this opinion. Bromel interprets the story of **Osiris** being torn apart by **Typhon** as a reference to Mosaic history—specifically that part which describes the Egyptian infanticide <note>A reference to the death of the firstborn in Egypt during the tenth plague.</note> perpetrated by the Exterminating Angel.

->That the Egyptians did not attribute eternity to matter<-

I shall remain silent on how the opinion of this most learned man <note>Referring to scholars like John Spencer or Maimonides, mentioned on previous pages, who argued for the extreme antiquity of Sabian culture.</note> suffers from a preconceived notion regarding the antiquity of the **Sabians** <note>original: "Zabiorum"; a group often identified by medieval and early modern scholars as ancient star-worshippers or the precursors to various "heresies."</note>. Since this notion is supported by very weak pillars, the whole mass of conclusions built upon it must necessarily collapse.

**XXI.** These, then, are the principal nations of Asia and Africa that devoted their efforts to philosophy. I have no doubt that other nations, taught by them, expressed the teachings of their masters through imitation, although this can hardly be demonstrated from the very few remains and ruins of their monuments that survive. Leaving these behind, we shall descend to more recent times to show briefly—and without following a strict order—how the modern peoples of the East have stubbornly followed in the footsteps of their ancestors. This was understood by **WINDETUS** <note>James Windet (d. 1664), an English physician and scholar of ancient theology.</note> in *On the State of the Departed*, page 40, using these words: *“No heresy is recorded to have ever spread so widely; namely, that **Duality of principles** <note>original: "Dualitas principiorum"; the belief in two co-eternal or opposing forces of Good and Evil.</note> (as the Arabs call it), which can be recognized even today by clear traces throughout the whole East as far as India and China.”*

**LAMBERT DANEAU** <note>A prominent 16th-century French Calvinist theologian.</note> also says in his notes on **AUGUSTINE’S** *On Heresies*, chapter 46, folio 119: *“It flourished and was most powerful in Arabia, Persia, and Egypt, from whence **Muhammadanism** <note>original: "Mahumetismus"; an archaic Western term for Islam. The author reflects the historical view that Islam incorporated elements of earlier Eastern dualism or "heresies."</note> was later born and hatched, as if from the egg of a serpent or viper, and persisted for a very long time. For even in the times of the Emperor **Anastasius**, it was still openly spreading in Persia, Mesopotamia, and Syria; and during the Papacy of **Gregory the Great**—that is, more than 340 years after the death of **Mani** <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the founder of Manichaeism, a religion based on the struggle between a good world of light and an evil world of darkness.</note>—it was still present in Sicily, as is apparent from Gregory...”*

Therefore, they attempt nothing, perform no action, nor undertake any journey or prepare for battle against enemies, unless this evil principle has been summoned into their counsel. For this reason, the demon is evoked with a solemn rite, and through his favor they sometimes predict things that the human mind could not otherwise foresee.

VOSSIUS describes on page 58 an illustrious example of this superstition, received from **ARCISZEWSKI** as an **eyewitness** <note>original Greek: "αὐτόπτη" (autoptē)</note>. This passage has been challenged without good reason by the learned **NICOLAS DE LANGES** <note>A 16th-century French magistrate and scholar.</note> (in *Epiphyllides*, Book 5, Chapter 15) and **PITHOU** <note>Pierre Pithou (1539–1596), a French lawyer and scholar.</note> (in *Miscellaneous Notes*, Book 5, Chapter 4), who substitute the name of **Belenus** <note>A Celtic sun god often equated with Apollo.</note> for Tibilenus—a change to which even Vossius was not opposed. 

And as the Romans saw two beings affected by divine honor from the Germans in this way, they judged that this should be interpreted as the worship of **Castor and Pollux** <note>The divine twins of Greek and Roman mythology, also known as the Dioscuri.</note>, whom they themselves venerated, as **TACITUS** <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian who wrote "Germania," an ethnographic study of Germanic tribes.</note> testifies in his *Book on the Customs of the Germans*: "Among the Naharvali," he says <note>original: "inquit"</note>, "a site of ancient religion is shown. A priest presides in feminine dress, but by Roman interpretation, they record the Gods as Castor and Pollux." <meta>This page continues the discussion on whether ancient poets viewed matter as eternal. It specifically focuses on Hesiod and Orpheus, investigating whether they should be classified as "Materialists" who believed that even the gods emerged from a pre-existing, eternal substance like Chaos or the Ocean.</meta>

(109)

...he will be judged to have been entirely free [from the charge of making God the source of evil], if it becomes certain—as many are convinced—that the **Ascræan Poet** <note>Hesiod, named for his birthplace, Ascra.</note> established his **Chaos** as eternal. Indeed, this seems most likely to me, because he does not seem to have easily departed from the teachings of **ORPHEUS**. It is the opinion of the Scholiasts, and specifically of **TZETZES** <note>John Tzetzes, a 12th-century Byzantine scholar known for his extensive commentaries on ancient Greek literature.</note>, that Hesiod expressed his own *Works and Days* <note>original: "Ἔργων καὶ ἡμερῶν" (Ergon kaihemeron)</note> in imitation of Orpheus’s books. From this, it is clear that Hesiod was not ignorant of other writings attributed to Orpheus.

Furthermore, that Orpheus believed not only that matter was eternal, but that it was also the cause of evils, appears even from that famous verse of his which celebrates the **unenviable necessity of ancient chaos** <note>original: "ἀρχαίς χάεος ἀμέγαρτος ἀνάγκη" (archais chaeos amegartos ananke). In ancient philosophy, "Necessity" often referred to the stubborn, uncreated properties of matter.</note>. As will become clear in what follows, this last word—"necessity"—was customarily used to designate matter. 

Meanwhile, I confess these things are quite uncertain, since it is well known that the writings circulated under the name of Orpheus should be attributed to others rather than to this Thracian poet himself. Thus, we cannot be entirely certain or confirmed regarding the actual opinion of Orpheus. 

For the rest, concerning that Chaos of Hesiod, one should consult **DICKINSON** in his *Ancient and True Physics*, Book V, § 2, and following; **BURNET** in his *Philosophical Archaeologies*, Book II, Chapter 1; and especially **BAYLE** <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), author of the influential *Historical and Critical Dictionary*.</note> in Volume III of his *Dictionary*, page 2856 (in the note) and page 2274, and following. This is because they did not set out to argue carefully about the natural principles of things—and thus about matter and the entire structure of creation—so much as they intended to discuss the **efficient cause**, God. <note>In philosophy, the "efficient cause" refers to the agent or force that actually brings something into being, as opposed to the "material cause," which is the physical substance things are made of.</note> For this reason, they were distinguished by the name of **Theologians** from the **Ionians**, who were called **Physicists** because of their more accurate investigation of natural causes. Therefore, the author of *Observation 21* (found in Volume 2 of the *Selected Halle Observations*, page 446) seems to me to pronounce more freely and confidently than is proper when he says: *“In this doctrine, however, they agreed—a doctrine common to all paganism—that they set eternal matter alongside God.”*

### XXVIII.

Moving from the mythical theology of the Greeks to the non-mythical, we turn at the start to their Ionian school, of which **THALES** is established as the <term>founder <note>original Greek: "archēgos" (ἀρχηγὸς), meaning a leader, first cause, or originator.</note></term> or Leader by **LAERTIUS**. <note>Diogenes Laertius was a famous biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> That school, moreover, is rightly distinguished into two classes. The first includes those who admitted only a single principle of things; the second contains those who, with **ANAXAGORAS** as their leader, acknowledged a God as the efficient cause in the production of the universe in addition to matter. To the former belong **THALES**, **ANAXIMANDER**, and **ANAXIMENES**; to the latter, **ANAXAGORAS**, **DIOGENES**, and **ARCHELAUS**. **DIOGENES LAERTIUS** <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers whose work is a primary source for the lives of ancient thinkers.</note> agrees in Book VIII, section 25, of *Lives of the Philosophers*. **PORPHYRY** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and biographer of Pythagoras.</note> commands us to establish nothing else in his *Life of Pythagoras*: *And thus [he calls] the principle of unity, and that of identity and equality, the cause of harmony, sympathy, and the preservation of the whole, which remains always the same...*

Nevertheless, he argues Pythagoras could have attributed unity to the atom insofar as it is the first principle of the simplest composition.

If we trust the notes of **Heinsius** <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a prominent Dutch scholar who edited the works of Maximus Tyrius.</note> on **Maximus Tyrius** <note>A 2nd-century AD rhetorician and philosopher whose lectures attempted to harmonize Platonic and earlier Greek thought.</note>, the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for their focus on mathematics and the dualism between the "Limited" and the "Unlimited."</note> gave the Greeks the first occasion for arriving at these principles. > O divine ones, from where did you come? From where did you become such?
> O men, from where did you come? From where did you become so evil?

From this there flowed the question: **If God makes good things, from where do evil things come?**

The belief that matter was not made by God but existed eternally alongside Him.</note> to Plato. 

Thus **TERTULLIAN** says in *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 15: *“Come now,” he says, “let the Pythagoreans learn, let the Stoics recognize, and Plato himself, from where Matter—which they wish to be uncreated—derived both its origin and its substance.”* <note>original: "Age nunc, inquit, discant Pythagorici, agnoscant stoici, Plato ipse unde Materia, quam innatam volunt, & originem & substantiam traxerit."</note>

He was convinced that Hierocles, having read the records of the Christians and being learned in their discipline, recognized the vanity of uncreated matter and took pains to persuade his readers that his Master [Plato] had not established a view that would be utterly contrary to both divine power and majesty. 

**JAQUELOT** supports Bayle in his *Examination of Baylean Theology*, published in French not long ago, *Part I, chapter 10, page 146.* These things are therefore certain: that in Plato's judgment, matter pre-existed; but it is no less certain and well-established that he added a "craftsman" <note>The "Demiurge," a divine figure in Platonic thought who fashions the universe out of pre-existing matter.</note> to this matter, who at some point approached its construction with full freedom—a point which is confirmed by the testimonies of many...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether Plato believed the world and matter were eternal or created. It moves from citing the Church Fathers to examining the testimonies of ancient biographers like Diogenes Laertius and later Neoplatonic interpreters who attempted to reconcile Plato's views with other philosophical systems.</meta>

(128)

This position stands, notably stated by **DIOGENES LAERTIUS** in Book III, Section 7, who says, according to Plato's mind: *“the world is one [and] created, since it is also perceptible, having been fashioned by God.”* <note>original Greek: "κόσμόν τε εἶναι... ἕνα γεννητὸν ἐπειδὴ καὶ αἰσθητός ἐστιν ὑπὸ θεοῦ κατεσκευασμένος." The Latin translation in the text reads: "mundum unum esse genitum... nam & sensibilis est a Deo conditus."</note>

Indeed, more recent Platonic teachers <note>The Neoplatonists of late antiquity.</note> altered this opinion using a completely different reasoning than **HIEROCLES**, and they wished to persuade others to believe that Plato established the world as being devoid of any beginning. **PROCLUS** is the primary proponent of this, as cited by <term>Raynaud</term> <note>Théophile Raynaud (1583–1663), a French Jesuit theologian known for his massive "Theologia Naturalis."</note> in *Natural Theology*, Distinction VIII, number 71, page 852. Add to these **AMELIUS** the Platonist <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist and student of Plotinus.</note> and certain Fathers mentioned in **HUET’S** *Alnetan Questions*, page 139. The <term>Pseudo-Origen</term> <note>Referring to the "Philosophumena," a work once attributed to Origen but now usually to Hippolytus of Rome.</note> in *The Philosopher*, page 111 of the Hamburg edition, seems to have followed these, saying: *“Matter is the principle and contemporaneous with God, and the world is uncreated.”* <note>original Greek: "τὴν μὲν οὖν ὕλην... ἀρχὴν εἶναι καὶ σύγχρονον τῷ θεῷ ταύτην καὶ ἀγέννητον τὸν κόσμον."</note> See what I have noted regarding that passage on page 112. It should not seem strange to us, however, since it is well known that the younger Platonists adapted as many of Plato’s dogmas as possible to suit either the doctrines of the Christians or even those of Aristotle. Compare **B. JACOB THOMASIUS** <note>Jakob Thomasius (1622–1684), a German philosopher and teacher of Leibniz.</note> in *On the Stoic Conflagration of the World*, page 37.

How God conducted Himself in working the matter is explained by **PLATO** himself in the *Timaeus*: *“God, wishing that all things should be good and nothing bad, insofar as it was within his power, took over everything that was visible—which was not at rest but moving discordantly and in disorder—and brought it into order out of disorder, judging that the former was in every way better than the latter.”* <note>original Greek: "βουληθεὶς ὁ θεὸς... ἀγαθὰ μὲν πάντα, φλαῦρον δὲ μηδὲν εἶναι... εἰς τάξιν αὐτὸ ἤγαγεν ἐκ τῆς ἀταξίας." This is a famous passage from Timaeus 30a describing the Demiurge (Creator) shaping pre-existing chaos.</note> **CICERO** translated these words thus:

<sig>I</sig>

<meta>catchword: τα</meta>

...expressed [it]: When God had decided to fill the world with the goods of all things, and to mix in no evil, as far as nature would allow; whatever existed that fell into the sense of sight, he took for himself, not calm and quiet, but immoderately agitated and fluctuating: and he brought this from disorder into order, for he judged this to be more excellent. Therefore, in that matter, Plato established an inordinate motion, which **PLUTARCH** also notes in *On the Generation of the Soul* <note>Latin title: *De Psychogonia*; a commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*.</note>, page 1014. "For there was a lack of order," he says, "before the generation of the world; a lack of order that was neither incorporeal, nor motionless, nor soulless; but having its bodily part formless and unstable, and its moving part frantic and irrational. This was the disharmony of a soul lacking reason." <note>original Greek: "Ἀκοσμία γὰρ ἦν... τὰ πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου γενέσεως, ἀκοσμία δὲ οὐκ ἀσώματος, οὐδὲ ἀκίνητος, οὐδὲ ἄψυχος· ἀλλὰ ἄμορφον μὲν καὶ ἀσύστατον τὸ σωματικόν, ἔμπληκτον δὲ καὶ ἄλογον τὸ κινητικὸν ἔχουσα. τοῦτο δ᾽ ἦν ἀναρμοστία ψυχῆς οὐκ ἐχούσης λόγον."</note> That is to say: certainly, before the world was born, matter was not devoid of body, motion, or soul, but was endowed with an informal and uncomposed body, and a reckless and brute motion: this very thing was the unfitness of a soul lacking proportion. 

Matter stubbornly resisted the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>From the Greek *demiourgos* (craftsman); the deity who fashions the physical world in Platonic philosophy.</note>, or God, who intended to bring this immoderate motion of matter into order, and even compelled God, however unwillingly, to leave seeds and traces of evil in the matter. For this reason, **PLATO** in the *Timaeus* (at the place cited) notes that God did not simply wish for evil, but [fashioned the world] "according to capacity," <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν</note> which **CICERO** well rendered as *as far as nature would allow*. In the same way, the disciples explain the Master's opinion. Hence **PLOTINUS** says in Book VIII of the first *Ennead*: "The nature of this world is indeed mixed, consisting of both Mind <note>Greek: *Nous*</note> and Necessity <note>Greek: *Ananke*</note>, and whatever comes into it from God is good." <note>original Greek: "μεμιγμένη... ἡ δὴ ἡ τοῦδε τοῦ κόσμου φύσις, ἔκ τε Νοῦ καὶ Ἀνάγκης, καὶ ὅσα παρὰ θεοῦ εἰς αὐτὸν ἥκει, ἀγαθά."</note>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the Platonic origins of evil. Having established in the previous page that matter was in a state of chaotic motion before the world was ordered, the author now provides evidence from various classical authorities—Plato, Seneca, Porphyry, and Chalcidius—to show that evil is not a creation of God, but a byproduct of the inherent resistance of "Necessity" or unformed matter.</meta>

<header>❦ (130) ❦</header>

Plato usually says: *“Evil things arise from that ancient nature, which he calls the whole underlying matter not yet ordered.”* <note>Original Greek: "τὰ δ' κακὰ ἐκ τῆς ἀρχαίας φύσεως τὴν ὅλην λέγειν τὴν ὑποκειμένην οὔπω κοσμηθεῖσαν εἴωθε"</note> That is: *The nature of this world exists as a mixture of Mind and Necessity; those things which proceed from God into the world are good, but evils arise from that ancient Nature, which* (**Plato**) *was accustomed to call the underlying matter not yet adorned.* Toward this point, **SENECA** addresses a question in the preface to Book I of his *Natural Questions*: *“Does God accomplish what He wills, or do the materials He handles fail Him in many things? Are many things formed poorly by the great Craftsman—not because His skill falters, but because the material upon which it is exercised is often disobedient to His art?”* From this, it is clear that Plato located the origin of evil in Matter, which **PORPHYRIUS** also implies in **PHOTIUS**, page 1315: *“And by necessity, vice also exists in the region around the earth.”* <note>Original Greek: "ἐξ ἀνάγκης δέ ἐστι καὶ ἡ κακία εἰς τὸν περὶ γῆν τόπον"</note> And **CHALCIDIUS** <note>A 4th-century translator and commentator on Plato's *Timaeus* whose work was the primary source of Platonic thought in the Latin West for centuries.</note>, on page 396, speaking from the mind of Plato, says: *“To the world, its good things were bestowed by the generosity of God, as if by a Father; but evils have clung to it through the fault of the mother—the forest <term>sylva</term> <note>The Latin word for "wood" or "forest," used by Chalcidius to translate the Greek word "hyle," which means both "wood" and "matter."</note>.”*

**MAXIMUS OF TYRE** interpreted Plato’s mind most extensively and perhaps even most accurately in his 25th Dissertation, where he is occupied with explaining this question: *“If God creates good things, from where do evil things come?”* <note>Original Greek: "εἰ Θεὸς τὰ ἀγαθὰ ποιεῖ, πόθεν τὰ κακά;"</note> His opinion comes down to this: good things are indeed from heaven, *“but evils arise from an innate wickedness; and this wickedness is twofold: one being an affection of matter, the other a license of the soul.”* <note>Original Greek: "τὰ δὲ κακὰ ἐξ ἀντοφυοῦς μοχθηρίας ἀνίστασθαι· διττὴν δὲ αὐτὴν, τὴν μὲν ὕλης πάθος, τὴν δὲ ψυχῆς ἐξουσίαν·"</note> That is, as interpreted by **HEINSIUS** <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a prominent Dutch scholar of the Renaissance.</note>: *“evils arise from the innate wickedness of the earth; and that wickedness is twofold: for it is either an affliction of corrupted matter, or the unrestrained freedom of the soul.”* Therefore, evil is twofold...

namely, he ascribes physical and moral [evil] to matter; the former to matter left to itself, but the latter to the soul, which is troubled by matter, as is clear from a more detailed explanation of his opinion. For he compares God to a craftsman engaged in shaping matter; if it is not correctly formed in every respect, he wishes that to be credited not to the craftsman, but to the material itself. These things indeed agree perfectly with **Plato’s** opinion: however, I fear that the disciple <note>Maximus of Tyre, a 2nd-century AD philosopher who considered himself a Platonist.</note> might depart from his Master, and furthermore, that he is not entirely consistent with himself, ascribing those things which he first thought should be attributed to matter to the deliberate plan of the Creator, referring evils to the conservation of the universe. <meta>This page continues the argument from page 131 regarding whether Maximus of Tyre is consistent with Platonic doctrine. The previous page questioned if Maximus strayed from Plato by suggesting that "evil" parts are necessary for the salvation of the whole universe; this page seeks to reconcile those views by citing Augustine and Justus Lipsius.</meta>

<page-num>132</page-num>

Indeed, AUGUSTINE speaks entirely according to the mind of the Stoics in his *Enchiridion*, chapter 101: *The highest good would not allow evil to be done, unless being omnipotent he was also able to make good out of evil.* <note>Original Latin: "Summe bonus non sineret fieri male, nisi omnipotens etiam de malo facere posset bene."</note> Compare chapters 10 and 96 of the same work, and the identical sayings of other Fathers found in GATAKER <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), an English scholar known for his edition of Marcus Aurelius.</note> on Book VI, 42 of *Antoninus’s* <note>The *Meditations* of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus.</note> books. Here, unless I am mistaken, MAXIMUS OF TYRE wished to imply the same thing, and thus he remains consistent with himself, and did not rashly stain his reputation with the mark of contradiction.

Finally, I cannot help but include an elegant passage on this argument by LIPSIUS <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a Flemish philosopher who sought to bridge Stoicism and Christianity.</note> from his *Physiology of the Stoics*, Book I, dissertation XIV, page 867: *Note that matter is unyielding, and from it come depraved things.* <note>Original Latin: "Nota materiam inobsequentem, & ab ea prava esse."</note> Plato often touches upon these things and moves toward this conclusion: *as when he says matter—or that which is in it—is an unruly and evil-doing soul,* <note>Original Greek: "ψυχὴν ἄτακτον καὶ κακοποιὸν"</note> *and again an adversary and rival to the beneficent Nature, that is, to God. He speaks of a soul or a force within matter: for he does not mean that matter is evil in itself, but that something hidden within it exerts and reveals itself during the process of creation.*

### XXXIII. 

These points are therefore settled: that Plato, besides God the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>From the Greek 'demiourgos', meaning a craftsman; in Platonic philosophy, the entity who fashions the physical universe out of pre-existing matter.</note> and author of good, established that matter is co-eternal and the fountain of all evil. For he denies in express words that God can be the author of any evil in the second book of the *Republic*, page 605, D: *Therefore God, since he is good, would not be the cause of all things, as the many say; but he is the cause of few things for men, and for many things he is not the cause. For the good things are much fewer than...* <note>Original Greek: "οὐδ᾿ ἄρα ὁ Θεὸς, ἐπειδὴ ἀγαθὸς, πάντων ἂν εἴη αἴτιος, ὡς οἱ πολλοὶ λέγουσιν· ἀλλ᾿ ὀλίγων μὲν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις αἴτιος, πολλῶν δὲ ἀναίτιος. Πολὺ γὰρ ἐλάττους τἀγαθὰ τῶν"</note>

XXXIV. Therefore, just as I distance myself from the opinion of those who think that **Plato** approaches most closely to the divine doctrine of the Christians on this point, I likewise profess my disagreement with a learned man—one who is praiseworthily diligent in explaining the opinions of the ancient philosophers—who recently in *Leisurely Collections* <note>original: "Otiis Fascic." refers to a scholarly miscellany or journal of the era.</note> II. p. 86, declared quite clearly that the **Platonic System** is no different from the **Spinozistic** one. But I do not believe this learned man will easily prove his opinion to anyone, since it is manifest that **Plato’s** God, in the creation and formation of this universe, does not so much "join and mix" himself with matter by the force of Platonic phrasing (as the **Stoics** assert), as he approaches it like a **god from a machine** <note>original: "ἀπὸ μηχανῆς" (apo mēchanēs). He adds in the same place that no distinction is observed between the systems of the **Stoics** and **Plato**, except that the latter attributed the union with matter to a soul separated from the supreme God, while the former attributed it to God himself.

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page, where the author refutes a contemporary scholar who claimed that Plato's system was identical to the pantheism of Baruch Spinoza. The previous page ended with a discussion of how Plato’s God relates to matter.</meta>

Furthermore, he <note>Referring to the "learned man" mentioned on the previous page who equated Plato with Spinoza.</note> attempts to prove that there is no difference between these systems by arguing that **Plato** judges the soul to be from the mind, and the mind from God, and thus these individual things do not differ in reality. He claims this is evident because **Plato** calls the world a "living being" and a "god."

First, it should be observed here that **Platonic** and **Stoic** <note>The Stoics were an ancient school of philosophy who believed that God was an immanent, physical force permeating the entire universe—a view often compared to later pantheism.</note> phrasings in this argument are very different and should not be combined thoughtlessly. Next, it is clear from various passages of **Plato** that he regarded the **World Soul** <term>anima mundi; the concept that the universe itself possesses a soul that directs its movements</term> as nothing other than a creature distinct from its Creator, although I would not dare deny that, following the lead of others, it seemed to him to be "plucked" from the divine essence.

He might call the world a "living being" <note>original: "animal." In this context, it refers to a being possessed of "anima" (soul or life-breath).</note> in the same sense that certain Church Fathers did—for example, **ORIGEN** in *On First Principles* <note>original Greek: "περὶ ἀρχῶν" (Peri Archon). Origen (c. 185–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> Book II, Chapter 1; **Tatian** in section 19; and others whom we know recoiled from the impious dreams of **Spinoza**. They did not fear to attribute a soul to the world and therefore call it by the name of a "living being."

Finally, I am still looking for the passage where **Plato** designated the world with the name "God." If such a passage were produced, **Plato** would be judged to have imitated the **Egyptians**, who likewise called the world "God," even though they confessed it was entirely different from God—indeed, that it was a created product. I do know this much, to hide nothing: the **Younger Platonists** <note>These are the Neoplatonists of late antiquity, who interpreted Plato's works through a more mystical and hierarchical lens.</note> explained their Master’s opinion as if he had established that the world, joined with its soul, occupies the third place in the divinity. ### XXXVI.

We proceed now to the **STOICS**, whom some have denied should be numbered among the **Dualists**, while others, moved by more than one argument, have more correctly affirmed it. **PLUTARCH** himself might seem to belong to the former class—those who deny Stoic dualism—since on page 370 of *On Isis and Osiris* <note>original: "de Isid. & Osir."</note>, where he tries to drag and snatch away every one of the ancient philosophers to his own side, he does not make even a single mention of the **Stoics**. ...from the admission of only two principles, namely matter and the good God, [it would follow] by a natural consequence. This is exactly what **Plutarch** <note>Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD) was a Middle Platonist who wrote several polemical works against the Stoics.</note> argued in his specific book *On Stoic Self-Contradictions* <note>original Greek: "περὶ Στωϊκῶν ἐναντιωμάτων"</note>, in order to demonstrate that the Stoics were not sufficiently consistent with themselves, and that they involved themselves in many difficulties that are not easily overcome. It is indeed common knowledge that the Stoics established two highest principles of things: one that acts, and the other that is acted upon. **Diogenes Laertius** <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers, likely writing in the 3rd century AD.</note> explains their thinking in Book VII, section 134 as follows: *It seems to them that there are two principles of the universe: the active and the passive. The passive, then, is the qualityless <term>apoion</term> substance, which is matter; while the active is the Reason <term>Logos</term> within it, which is God.*

**Seneca** <note>The Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman (c. 4 BC – 65 AD).</note> says almost the same thing in Epistle 65: *Our Stoics say, as you know, that there are two things in the nature of things from which all things are made: cause and matter. Matter lies inert, a thing ready for all things, destined to remain still if no one moves it. Cause, however—that is, Reason—shapes matter and turns it wherever it wishes.*

I do not wish to accumulate more citations, which can be read in **Menagius** <note>Gilles Ménage (1613–1692), a French scholar who wrote extensive commentaries on Diogenes Laertius.</note> on *Laertius VII, 134*, **Lipsius** <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), the Flemish humanist who revived Stoicism in the early modern period.</note> in *Stoic Physiology II, 4*, and **Gataker** <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), an English theologian and critic known for his edition of Marcus Aurelius.</note> on *Antoninus II, 2; IV, 21; V, 13; and VI, 32*.

They therefore subjected this matter to God, so that he could form from it whatever he wished according to his own will; on this matter, see **Antoninus** <note>The Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius (121–180 AD), author of the *Meditations*.</note> in Book VI, section 1. There is a famous passage by **Seneca** in chapter V of *On Providence*. "Why," he says, "*was God so unjust in the distribution of fate that he assigned poverty, wounds, and bitter deaths to good men?*" [He answers:] "*The craftsman cannot change the matter: it has endured [its own limitations]: certain things cannot be separated from others; they cohere and are indivisible.*" Compare the same author in the preface to *Natural Questions*.

All these things are confirmed by **Lipsius** <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a Flemish scholar who sought to harmonize Stoicism with Christianity.</note>, who was as knowledgeable about Stoic philosophy as anyone. For he says in his *Stoic Physics*, Book II, chapter 2, page 58: "*They make matter equally primary and eternal as God himself.*" Next he adds: "*This was the doctrine by the general consensus of the ancients. For if matter were born and created, it must necessarily have been made from something: but that 'something' would itself be matter.*"

For everyone accepted that famous saying of **Democritus**: *Nothing comes from nothing, and nothing is destroyed into nothingness.* <note>original Greek: "μηδὲν ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος γίγνεσθαι, μηδὲ εἰς τὸ μὴ ὂν φθείρεσθαι." This is a fundamental principle of ancient physics: the conservation of matter.</note> The same author [Lipsius] says in Book I, section 14, page 32, regarding matter being considered a "principle of evil" by this school of philosophers: "*I assert,*" he says, "*that the Stoics placed the principle of evil not in God, but in matter (which nevertheless was, as they themselves intended, co-eternal and equal in age to God)—in matter, I say, they established it. And so, when God made humans and other things, he fashioned everything good and for a good purpose, but [there was] some resistant force and...*"

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the Stoic view of matter. While the previous page suggested that matter’s inherent nature might limit God's power, this page clarifies the Stoic defense: that "evil" (like disease or physical fragility) is not a primary creation of God but a necessary side-effect of a beneficial design.</meta>

<header>❦ (155) ❧</header>

Just as **Marcus Aurelius** <note>Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (121–180 AD), the Roman Emperor and Stoic philosopher.</note> says in *Book VI, § 1*: "the substance of the whole is compliant and ready for change," <note>original Greek: ἡ τῶν ὅλων οὐσία εὐπειθὴς καὶ εὐτρεπὴς</note> that is, *the matter of the universe is obedient and ready to comply.* But these and other passages are not to be accepted without restriction; they seem to be interpreted as referring to the superior part of matter rather than to all of it. For it is clear that **Chrysippus** <note>A fundamental figure in Stoicism who formalized much of its doctrine.</note> himself placed the "fault" within matter, as is evident from the words cited by **Aulus Gellius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman author whose *Attic Nights* (Noctes Atticae) preserves fragments of earlier lost books.</note> from Book IV of *On Providence* in his *Attic Nights* (VI. 1). For here, inquiring whether providence afflicted humans with diseases, he judges that it was not the primary intention of nature to make men subject to diseases. *For this was never suitable for the author of nature and parent of all good things. But, he says, while she [Nature] was producing many great things, and was creating the most fit and useful things, other inconveniences were born at the same time, joined to those very things she was making.* He says these were produced not through nature's primary intent, but through certain necessary sequels, which he himself calls <term>by way of consequence</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ παρακολούθησιν (katà parakoloúthēsin). This is the Stoic theory that some "evils" are unavoidable side-effects of a greater good.</note>. *Just as, he says, when nature was forming human bodies, a more subtle reason and the very nature of the body required that she compose the head from very thin and small bones. But this utility of a greater thing was followed by a certain other external inconvenience: that the head was made poorly protected, and fragile to small blows and strikes.* Here we certainly see that the blame for evil is removed from God, the parent of all good things, and is attributed to certain necessary sequels or <term>consequences</term> <note>original Greek: παρακολουθήσεις</note>, which entirely agree with the passage of **Seneca** cited before, in which he says, *some things cannot be separated; they are connected and indivisible.* Next,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Stoic philosophy, transitioning from the previous page's focus on the limitations of God and the constraints of matter to the logical inconsistencies found in Stoic systems, particularly the tension between Fate and Free Will.</meta>

It was a common failing among the ancients to construct **systems** that were poorly held together; very few were concerned with the manner in which they could connect the opinions they defended and bring them into a proper order. This point is rightly observed by **Dr. Buddeus** <note>Johann Franz Buddeus (1667–1729), a prominent German Lutheran theologian and philosopher.</note> in his *Historical-Philosophical Miscellany*, page 322. The remarks of **Clericus** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a renowned Genevan theologian and scholar famous for his critical journals.</note> on this subject are most agreeable (*Bibliothèque Choisie*, Volume I, page 85): *“We often conjecture,”* he says, *“that an author held a certain opinion because it aligns with other views he approved of; conversely, we deny that another held a certain position because it fits poorly with his other beliefs. But in truth, it often happens that writers do not see the consequences that flow from certain opinions, nor do they understand that they are admitting doctrines that are mutually contradictory.”* And it is evident to everyone that this was especially characteristic of the **Stoics**—they would entangle themselves in their own logical knots because of their various doctrines, which sometimes met in direct opposition.

It becomes clear from many passages in the works of **Marcus Antoninus** <note>The Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius (121–180 AD), author of the *Meditations*.</note>, **Epictetus**, **Arrian** <note>Arrian of Nicomedia, the student who recorded the discourses of the philosopher Epictetus.</note>, and **Seneca** that this school of philosophers left human beings with free will. These passages have been collected by **Gataker** <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), an English cleric and scholar who published a highly regarded edition of Marcus Aurelius.</note> (in his commentary on *Antoninus* II. 9) and **Huet** <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar.</note> (*Alnetan Questions* II. 10, page 166 and following). **Epictetus** indeed attributes such power to this will that in Book I, Chapter 1 of his *Discourses*, he does not hesitate to say that <term>proæresin</term> <note>The Greek term *prohairesis* refers to the faculty of choice or moral purpose; the original text reads: "τὴν προαίρεσιν οὐδ᾽ ὁ Ζεὺς νικῆσαι δύναται"</note> "not even Jupiter himself can conquer." *See page 385 and following, and Critical Art, Volume 1, Part 2, page 424.*
**MERIC CASAUBON** <note>Meric Casaubon (1599–1671) was an English classical scholar and cathedral dignitary, known for his works on "enthusiasm" and credulity.</note> in his English book *On Credulity and Incredulity*, page 124 and following; and **B. STOLBERG** <note>Balthasar Stolberg (1640–1684), a German philologist.</note> in his dissertation on the *Logos* <note>original: "λόγῳ" - Word or Reason</note> and the *Mind* <note>original: "Νῷ" - Nous</note> of Plato, in his *Greek Exercises*, recently republished. "The better" <note>original: "βέλτιον"</note> is heard more often in the passages cited above from **PLUTARCH**. That he is called the "Craftsman" <note>original: "Δημιουργὸν" - Demiurge</note> is clear from the example of **ANAXAGORAS**, who called his "Mind" the Craftsman. Thus **CYRIL** <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father.</note> in *Against Julian*, Book 6, page 115, is our authority that **Julian** <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman Emperor.</note> said: "For our people say that the Craftsman of all things is the common father and king, but that the rest of the nations have been distributed by him to ethnic governors and city-protecting gods" <note>original: "οἱ γὰρ ἡμέτεροί φασι τὸν δημιουργὸν ἁπάντων μὲν εἶναι κοινὸν πατέρα καὶ βασιλέα, νενεμῆσθαι δὲ τὰ λοιπὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν ὑπ' αὐτοῦ ἐθνάρχαις καὶ πολιούχοις θεοῖς"</note>. **Plato** specifically called it the "beneficent soul" <note>original: "ψυχὴν ἀγαθουργὸν"</note> and "the same" <note>original: "ταὐτὸν"</note>, as was proved above by the testimony of *Plutarch*.

To this, moreover, belong all the names by which the pagans distinguished the supreme God from the inferior ones. For it must not be thought that the minds of the pagans were so dull and senseless that they persuaded themselves that so many Gods were equal in power and dignity. **ONATUS** the Pythagorean will serve as an example for all, whom **STOBAEUS** <note>Joannes Stobaeus, a 5th-century compiler of Greek philosophical extracts.</note> in his *Physical Eclogues*, Book 1, page 4, introduces speaking thus: "It seems to me that God is not just one, but there is one who is greatest and superior, and who rules over the whole; and the others differ greatly in power; and he reigns over them all, etc." <note>original: "δοκεῖ δέ μοι, καὶ μὴ εἷς εἶμεν ὁ θεὸς, ἀλλ' εἷς μὲν ὁ μέγιστος, καὶ καθυπέρτερος, καὶ ὁ κρατέων τῶ παντὸς, οἱ δ' ἄλλοι πολὺ διαφέροντες κατὰ δύναμιν' βασιλεύει δὲ πάντων αὐτῶν &c."</note> Hence, "fellow-rulers with God" <note>original: "συνάρχοντες θεῷ"</note> are mentioned by **MAXIMUS TYRIUS** <note>A 2nd-century Platonist philosopher and rhetorician.</note> and "fellow-rulers with the greatest spirit" <note>original: "τῷ μεγίστῳ δαίμονι συνάρχοντες" - note that 'daimon' here refers to a divine spirit or lesser god, not a 'demon' in the modern sense.</note> by **PLATO**. Many Doctors of the primitive Church recognized and praised this, such as **Tertullian** in his *Apology*.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Principles" recognized by ancient philosophers. Having previously discussed the titles given to the supreme Good Principle, the author now transitions to how Plato and other thinkers characterized "Matter" (hylē) as the receptive, maternal, and sometimes resistant substance of the universe.</meta>

(164)
<meta>catchword: Plato</meta>

Plato and others following his example deign to call that **matter** <note>original Greek: ὕλην (*hylēn*)</note> by other names, calling it the <term>Mother and Receptacle of all that is created, visible, and perceptible</term> <note>original Greek: τὴν τοῦ γεγονότος ὁρατοῦ καὶ παντὸς αἰσθητοῦ Μητέρα καὶ ὑποδοχήν (*tēn tou gegonotos horatou kai pantos aisthētou Mētera kai hypodochēn*)</note>. Thus **PLUTARCH** <note>A Greek historian and philosopher (c. 46–120 AD).</note> says in Volume II of his *Works*, page 1015, in the treatise *On the Generation of the Soul*: "For Plato calls matter both Mother and Nurse." That is: *Plato indeed calls matter the mother and the nurse.* A twin passage exists in the *Philosophies* of **Pseudo-ORIGEN** <note>Likely referring to the *Philosophumena* or *Refutation of All Heresies*, now generally attributed to Hippolytus of Rome rather than Origen.</note>, chapter 19, page 109 of the Hamburg edition: "...and all the underlying matter, which he calls both the receptacle and the nurse, from which, once organized, the four elements proceeded." That is: *truly the universal underlying matter, which he calls both the receptacle and the nurse, from which the four elements, having been arranged, came forth.* 

I have noted in my remarks that **MENAGIUS** <note>Gilles Ménage (1613–1692), a French scholar known for his commentaries on ancient philosophy.</note> unreasonably disturbed this passage by reading *Tethys* <note>A sea goddess in Greek mythology.</note> instead of "nurse" <note>original Greek: τιθήνην (*tithēnēn*)</note>, and I am not a little confirmed in this judgment by the passage from Plutarch just cited. **CHALCIDIUS** <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his Latin translation and commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*.</note> embraced all these names when, on page 370, he calls matter the "mother," "little nurse," and the "womb of all generation." 

**SERVIUS** <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, a 4th-century grammarian famous for his commentary on Virgil.</note> says that matter is "Generality" in his commentary on Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book III, page 267—perhaps following the example of Plato, who (according to the Scholiast on Hesiod’s *Theogony*) called Chaos "the all-receiving," that is, *receiving all things*. Compare **WINDET** <note>James Windet (d. 1664), an English physician and scholar who wrote on the state of the soul after death.</note> in *On the State of the Departed*, page 51. That matter was likewise known as <term>Necessity</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνάγκη (*anankē*)</note>; this was undoubtedly for the reason that the depraved condition of matter did not permit everything to be corrected or set right, and thus a place was necessarily left for evil and depravity.

the word **spirit** <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα (*pneuma*)</note> being understood, as **LAMBERT BOS** <note>Lambert Bos (1670–1717) was a Dutch scholar famous for his work on Greek "ellipses"—words omitted but understood by the reader.</note> reminds us (in *Greek Ellipsis*, p. 101), it is accepted everywhere as referring to the good and supreme God, and specifically in the writings of **AELIAN** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric (c. 175–235 AD) who wrote in Greek.</note> (*Various History*, VI. 13) and **PHALARIS** <note>The "Letters of Phalaris" were long attributed to a 6th-century BC Sicilian tyrant, though later proven to be forgeries from the 2nd century AD.</note> (Epistle 3). <meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the dualism of ancient cosmology. I have [the work of] **WINDET** <note>James Windet (d. 1664) was an English physician and scholar. His work *Stromateus Epistolikos* (1663) discussed the state of the soul after death and is the source being cited here.</note>, page 34. *According to the Greeks, he says, the Craftsman God is called **Zeus** <note>original Greek: ζεὺς (*Zeus*)</note>, and in his power is life; Matter is called **Hades** <note>original Greek: ᾅδης (*Hades*)</note>, in whose power is death or dissolution: Thus all things are either **in the realm of Zeus** <note>original Greek: ἐν Διὸς (*en Dios*)</note> or **in the realm of Hades** <note>original Greek: ἐν Ἅιδῃ (*en Haide*)</note>. Zeus, to whom light and day yield their authority, has **Friendship** <note>original Greek: Φιλίαν (*Philian*)</note> or **Love** <note>original Greek: Ἔρωτα (*Erota*)</note> as his servant—Hades has **strife as a subordinate** <note>original Greek: νεῖκος ὑπῶργον (*neikos hypourgon*)</note>, whose forces are enwrapped in darkness and **disappearance** <note>original Greek: ἀφανισμῷ (*aphanismo*)</note>: for Hades is the privation of light, according to the Etymologist, Plutarch, Plato, etc.*

### XL.

Having thus traversed the entire choir of ancient philosophers, we come to the Christians. It is astounding that some of them could be so immersed in and utterly swallowed by the shadows of this error, despite being in such great light of heavenly doctrine. But such was the human mind's sometimes detestable perversity and sometimes deplorable weakness, that the first followers of Christ's sacred rites began to adapt many errors—which they saw sprouting in the fields of the pagans <term>gentilium</term>—to themselves, and they resolved to strike a bargain between light and darkness.
