In this matter, however, I agree with the late **BARTOLD HINCKELMANN** <note>A German theologian (1648–1695) and scholar of Oriental languages.</note> that verse 18 <note>Referring to Colossians 2:18.</note>—concurring with **BENEREGIUS** <note>Johannes Benediktus Carpzov II (1639–1699), a famous professor at Leipzig; "Beneregius" is a Latinized form of his name.</note> in Part II of the *Great Synod*, page 196—should be interpreted as the **worship of angels** introduced into the Church by Simon. This is especially true after the highly reverend **CASPAR NEUMANN** <note>A German professor and hymn writer (1648–1715).</note>, in his *Dissertation on the Palm Not to Be Overturned by the Angelics* (Wittenberg, 1692), demonstrated it with arguments beyond all objection. 

I am not unaware, however, that the late **JOHANN ADAM SCHERTZER** in his *System of Theology*, page 104, along with **ROBERT BELLARMINE** <note>A Jesuit Cardinal (1542–1621) and one of the most important figures in the Counter-Reformation.</note> in book I of *On the Holiness of the Blessed*, chapter 20, and **ALPHONSO SALMERON** <note>A Spanish Jesuit (1515–1585) and one of the founding members of the Society of Jesus.</note> in volume 15 of his *Works*, folio 348, accuse those asserting this of error. They cite the Jesuit **JUSTINIANUS** <note>Benedictus Justinianus (1550–1622), a Jesuit biblical commentator.</note> as being **of the same mind** <note>original Greek: ὁμοψήφῳ (*homopsēphō*)</note> and call upon history to defend their opinion. 

But that Simon Magus raised the standard for the worship of angels is rightly proved against **BARONIO** <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), an Italian cardinal and the father of Catholic ecclesiastical history.</note> (*Annals*, volume I, for the year 6, number 17) by **DENIS PÉTAU** <note>A French Jesuit theologian (1583–1652) known for his work on the history of dogma.</note> in his *Notes on Epiphanius*, page 40, and by **NOEL ALEXANDRE** <note>A French Dominican theologian (1639–1724) and church historian.</note> in *First Century*, chapter 10, page 52. It is placed beyond controversy by **TERTULLIAN** <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD) often called the "father of Latin theology."</note> in *The Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 33.

If the interpretation of Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a Church Father best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> is granted a place, we would find a new trace of Zoroaster or the Magi <note>Persian priests and practitioners of Zoroastrianism.</note> in the error of Basilides. For Jerome notes in his commentary on *Amos, chapter III*, that the mystical name—according to the Greek letters and the number of the annual cycle—is contained within the circle of the sun; the pagans called this same number, using different letters, **Mithras** <note>The Persian god of the sun; in Greek gematria, both "Abraxas" and "Meithras" add up to 365.</note>. Various authors have shown this through different methods of calculation, regarding whom see Ittig in the place cited, page 101. 

Now indeed, it is established from the above that the Persian Magi pursued the solemn worship of Mithras as a symbol of the "good principle," which Basilides seems quite rightly to have expressed through imitation. Stephen Morin <note>A 17th-century French Protestant theologian and linguist.</note> was certainly convinced that this was a mystical name for the sun in his *Exercise on the Primitive Language*, Exercise I, chapter 13, page 131, thinking it was derived from the Hebrew word *Abrech* <note>original: אברך, a term found in Genesis 41:43, often translated as 'bow the knee' or as a title of honor given to Joseph.</note>. Jerome's conjecture also seems not improbable to that man of skillful genius, **CAVE** <note>William Cave (1637–1713), an English church historian.</note>, in his *Literary History* under the entry for **Basilides**.

**XLVI. CARPOCRATES**, or as others call him, **Carpocras**, we rightly join to Basilides <note>Basilides was an early Gnostic teacher in Alexandria; the previous pages detailed his complex system of 365 heavens.</note>, as he is judged not to be separated from him in his opinions. For he, no less than the others we have considered, believed the world was created by Angels and primarily by the Devil; he called the supreme God "the Father of all things, unknown and unnamed," according to the authorities **IRENAEUS** and **EPIPHANIUS** <note>Irenaeus (2nd century) and Epiphanius (4th century) were "heresiologists"—writers who documented and argued against sects they considered heretical.</note>. Nor did he, along with his companions, distance himself from a life polluted by the worst filth of vices, but following the example of his predecessors, he joined impurity of life with the filth of his dogmas. By this very act, he diminished the reputation of Christians among the gentiles <note>The "gentiles" here refers to the non-Christian Roman/pagan public.</note> to no small degree, a fact which **EUSEBIUS** left witnessed in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, Chapter 7.

The **ADAMITES** or **Adamiani**, as they are called by Augustine and Epiphanius, are a branch of the Carpocratians (see **DANEAU** <note>Lambert Daneau (c. 1530–1595), a French Calvinist theologian who edited Augustine's works.</note> on *Augustine's On Heresies, 31*). They adopted not only the same dogma but also a detestable way of living as its perpetual companion. The former is witnessed by the author of the *List of Heresies* <note>original: *Indiculus haeresium*; a catalog of deviant beliefs.</note> (which some wrongly attribute to Jerome: see the preface of **ITTIG** <note>Thomas Ittig (1643–1710), a Lutheran theologian and historian of the early church.</note> to his *Book on Heresiarchs*, §. 4). In chapter 14, he reports that they established "two substances" in the same way that others established "two principles" <note>This refers to Dualism, the belief in two opposing forces, such as Good and Evil or Spirit and Matter.</note>. Nor should this seem surprising, since they undoubtedly either drew this from or confirmed it with the books of **Zoroaster** <note>The ancient Persian prophet; Gnostic groups often claimed his ancient authority to legitimize their own dualistic views.</note>, whose possession they particularly boasted of, as **CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA** writes in *Stromata*, Book III, page 319. This was something that surely not even the heretics of that age had dared to do until then, as I proved on page 403, note 7. Compare the work *On Florinus* by ITTIG, page 131; DODWELL on the *Leaders of Heresy* in the place cited; and FORBES, book 1, chapter 37 of his *Instruction on Theological History*, page 70 and following. As for **BARDESANES**, the disciples of this follower of *Valentinus* show that he also approved of his master's dogma. One of these disciples, named *Marinus*, says that he and his fellow believers are distinguished from the orthodox by three main points, according to **ORIGEN** in his *Dialogue on the Right Faith in God*, section 3. The first of these is that they deny the Devil was created by God. From this, it is not gathered in vain that they established Satan as equal to God. Nor did **PTOLEMY** wander far from this among the first of Valentinus's disciples, establishing that the Law proceeded from the "demiurge" <note>A Gnostic term for the "craftsman" or lesser deity who created the physical universe</note> or creator of this universe, as is clear from his letter which appears in **EPIPHANIUS**, *Heresy 33*, and which has been published in a more corrected version in **GRABE’S** *Spicilegium*, Volume II, page 69. Compare BUDDEUS *On the Valentinian Heresy*, page 485, regarding him. That the rest of *Valentinus's* disciples stuck in the same mire <note>original: "eodem cœno," a metaphor for being bogged down in the same filthy or muddled errors</note> will be clear from the celebrated ITTIG’S *Dissertation on the Leaders of Heresy*, chapter 6, and Dr. BUDDEUS’S *Dissertation on the Valentinian Heresy*, page 482 and following.

Report says of **CERDO** <note>A Syrian Gnostic teacher who moved to Rome around 140 AD; he taught that the God of the Old Testament was different from the God of the New Testament</note>, it shows something else regarding him, saying that there are three principles <note>term: *archai* (ἀρχάς), meaning the fundamental origins or first causes of the universe</note>. ## XLIX.

Marcion found many supporters of this error among his disciples, whom I do not wish to enumerate in full here out of a desire for brevity. In this respect, therefore, Apelles differs from Marcion: for while the former [Marcion] established three principles <note>While Marcion is often called a dualist, some ancient commentators argued he proposed three principles: the Good God, the Just Creator, and the Evil Matter</note>, Apelles admits only two; furthermore, those two are not equal and co-eternal—as Marcion claimed of his own—but are instead subordinate to one another.

## L.

Now there appears before us not just a single sectarian, but an entire troop of heretics, who are called **GNOSTICS** <term>Gnostics: derived from the Greek word *gnosis*, meaning "knowledge." These groups claimed to possess a secret, superior knowledge necessary for salvation</term> because of their "falsely so-called knowledge" and the doctrine drawn from **SIMON** [Magus] and the rest of the deceivers. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the origins and terminology of Gnosticism, moving from the specific doctrines of Apelles to a broader debate among historians regarding whether "Gnostic" was a contemporary label or a later invention. ...tracing back to **Carpocrates** <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and founder of a Gnostic sect known for advocating a form of libertinism</note>, a matter which **ITTIGIUS** <note>Thomas Ittig (1643–1710), a German Lutheran theologian and influential church historian</note> discussed extensively and learnedly in chapter IX, page 162 and following; and before him **G. J. VOSSIUS** <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar and theologian</note> in his *Fragment on the Manichaeans* <note>original: *fragmento de Manich.*</note>, which appears in Volume VI of his *Collected Works* <note>original: *Opp.*, short for *Opera*</note>, page 833. However, we shall not take up this dispute ourselves, since most agree that **Simon** <note>Simon Magus, a figure from the New Testament (Acts 8) traditionally regarded by the Church Fathers as the first heretic</note> and the heretics following in his footsteps are rightly included under the name of **Gnostics** if they are judged by the opinions they held in common with the Gnostics specifically so called. Conversely, others who were distinct from all of those groups are no less rightly distinguished from them by the name of Gnostics, as it was specifically in the 2nd century, under **Pope Anicetus** <note>Bishop of Rome from c. 155 to 166 AD; his reign saw many Gnostic teachers arrive in Rome</note>, that they chose to be called by this name.

Histor.*, likely referring to Christian Thomasius, a jurist and philosopher</note>, section 31; by **DANÆUS** <note>Lambert Daneau (c. 1530–1595), a French Reformed theologian who commented on early Christian writings</note> in his commentary on Augustine's *On Heresies*, chapter VI, page 67; and by **ITTIGIUS** in the passage cited above, page 165. For this reason, the reasoning of **ARNOLD** <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a radical pietist historian who famously argued that many "heretics" were actually truer Christians than the established Church</note> is entirely inconsistent when he classifies this specific title of "Gnostics" among "more recent figments of the brain" and mocks it falsely on page 71 of the first volume of his *History of Heresies* <note>original: *Hæresiolog.*</note>. He seems to have done this for no other purpose than to use a striking example to confirm his preconceived opinion that "heretics" and "heresies" were merely invented or falsified by the ancient era.

Besides him, **Jacob Philipp Hartmann** in his work *On the Deeds of Christians under the Apostles* <note>original: *de rebus gestis Christianorum sub Apostolis*</note>, page 572, likewise denies that the Gnostics formed a distinct sect. However, we are not concerned with those arguments at present; our current task is to prove that this "filth of sectarians" <note>original: *sectariorum colluviem*; a common polemical term for groups deemed heretical</note> was also submerged in this same mire <note>Likely referring to the moral or theological corruption the author is attempting to link to these groups</note>.

It critiques historians like Gottfried Arnold who viewed "heresy" as a later fabrication by the early Church.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into Gnostic sects, specifically examining their dualistic theology (the belief in two opposing gods) and their alleged connection to the teachings of Zoroaster and ancient occultism.</meta>

This is indeed witnessed by **AUGUSTINE** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers</note> in his work *On Heresies*, chapter 6: *"They are also said,"* he writes, *"to hold in their teachings both a good God and an evil God."* Similarly, **EPIPHANIUS** <note>Bishop of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), known for his 'Panarion', a massive encyclopedia of heresies</note> reports in *Heresies* 26, page 91, that they represent the ruler of this world in the likeness of a **Dragon**, by whom souls are swallowed up if they are destitute of that knowledge <note>The Greek word 'Gnosis', which the Gnostics claimed was the secret key to salvation</note>.

While these facts are certain, those points suspected by **CHRISTIAN LUPUS** <note>Christian Wolf (1612–1681), a Flemish theologian and historian of church councils</note> in his *Commentary on Tertullian’s 'On the Prescription of Heretics', chapter 13*, seem more doubtful. Lupus—contradicting himself—suspects that the African, Rhodan <note>referring to the region of the Rhône in modern-day France</note>, and Eastern Churches added the word *one* to the words of the **Apostles' Creed** (*"I believe in [one] God"*) specifically so that the Gnostic error regarding a "double God" might be refuted. Compare this with **PEARSON** <note>John Pearson (1613–1686), an English bishop whose 'Exposition of the Creed' is a landmark of Anglican theology</note> in his *On the Apostles' Creed*, page 39.

This same connection is confirmed by the fact that they held the name of **Zoroaster** <note>The ancient Persian prophet and founder of Zoroastrianism, often associated by early Christians with magic and dualism</note> in the highest regard, as if they were fervent followers of his error; so much so that they boasted of possessing the secret books of this Magus, according to **CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA** <note>A prominent Christian teacher (c. 150–215 AD) who sought to reconcile Greek philosophy with Christianity</note> in *Miscellanies, Book I, page 63*. Indeed—what carries even more weight—**BARONIUS** <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a cardinal and historian who wrote the 'Annales Ecclesiastici' to defend the Catholic Church</note> in *Annals, Volume II, folio 80, for the year 120 AD*, reports from **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of Christianity</note> that the Gnostics in Rome published books under the title *The Revelations of Zoroaster*.

Connected to these same errors were other beliefs that pleased them: namely, that the substance of the soul is divine (witnessed by **AUGUSTINE** in *Heresy 6*), and that **Christ was clothed in a phantom body** <note>This is the doctrine of Docetism—the belief that Jesus only appeared to be human but was actually a purely spiritual being</note>, as witnessed by **EPIPHANIUS** in *Heresy 26*. Nor did they hide the filth of their lifestyle from their doctrine, which they defiled with various and most wicked lusts; **Epiphanius** explains these at length in the place cited above, as he was at one time an <term>eyewitness <note>original Greek: αὐτόπτης (autoptes)</note></term> to them. His reliability, however, was questioned by **HERALDUS** <note>Desiderius Heraldus (c. 1575–1649), a French legal scholar and critic</note>...

LI. This collection of wretchedness leads us to another class of heretics, most of whom were called **Docetists** <term>Docetae: from the Greek 'dokein' (to seem), referring to the belief that Jesus only appeared to be human</term>, **Phantasiadocetists**, **Anthropomorphists**, or—named after the leader and restorer of the heresy—**Marcionites** <note>Followers of Marcion of Sinope, who believed the physical world was the work of an inferior or evil deity and therefore rejected Christ’s physical nature</note>. For since these people intended to deny the human nature of Christ, they rendered it imaginary. They established that it was either brought down and assembled from heaven or from the elements, or at least that it was a mere shadow; in doing so, they certainly raised suspicion of nearly the same error regarding themselves. Indeed, they seem to have arrived at the opinion that the body was either produced by an active **evil principle** <term>the 'efficient principle' refers to the primary source or creator of a thing</term>, or was forged from matter that originated from evil. However, since their sense of piety commanded them to declare Christ free from the filth of vices, and because of their conviction that he was the restorer of a world that was corrupt in itself, it was impossible for them not to strip Christ of any true physical body. In concluding this, I am moved especially by the reason that all those among the Christians who defended that wicked dogma of **two principles** <note>the dualist belief in two co-eternal, opposing gods: one of good/spirit and one of evil/matter</note> also showed that they did not consider this error un-

LII. **HERMOGENES** <note>A late 2nd-century teacher and painter from Carthage who sought to explain the existence of evil through the nature of matter.</note> certainly belongs to the class of those who, while attributing the creation of the universe to one and the same God, and being anxious about the origin of evil, posited that matter was co-eternal with God. **TERTULLIAN** sharply refuted this error—which was derived from the **Stoic Schools**—in a specific book pertaining to the examination of the heresy of Hermogenes. His disciples and supporters are called <term>Materiarii</term> <note>From the Latin word for "matter." But I cannot hide the fact that various difficulties in this chapter of history are frequently raised by scholars. For **THEODORET** <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458/466), a bishop and influential theologian of the Byzantine Church.</note> in Book I, chapter 26 of his *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, and **Suidas** in his *Lexicon* under the entry for *Manes*, seem to identify this Scythianus as being the same person as Manes. **EPIPHANIUS** also counts **Origen** <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), one of the most prolific early Christian theologians, who actually died before Manichaeism became a major movement.</note> among those who opposed the errors of Manes; yet there can be no doubt that Origen passed away before the birth of Manes. This cannot be true, for if it were, Scythianus would have to be separated from Manes by a far greater span of time than the authority of the ancient writers allows.

These points and others of less importance are urged especially by **ARNOLD** <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a radical Pietist historian who often defended "heretics" against the established church accounts.</note> on page 127 (following the lead of others), so that he might further preoccupy the reader's mind and make it certain that the stories told about the Manichaeans are entirely unreliable.

**LIV.** From these matters, I believe it is clear that the error of **Manes** was drawn in **Persia**, and should be derived from the **Magi** <term>Magi: Ancient Persian priests and scholars of the Zoroastrian religion, often associated by Western writers with dualism (the battle between light and dark)</term> rather than from the **Greek philosophers** or from the heretics who preceded him. That is: *that he established two principles, which also lacked a beginning, nor would they ever end, and were mutually contrary, one of which he called light and good: the other darkness and evil, so that they are the same as God and the Devil: whom indeed he sometimes named both as Gods, namely a good God and an evil God. From these two principles all things arose and were constituted; from one of which all good things proceed, and from the other all evil things, which have their subsistence in this world from both principles. Nor does **ARNOLD** <note>Gottfried Arnold, the historian being criticized throughout this section.</note> (on page 124) dare to deny this entirely, though you may wonder that he asserts these crimes belonged only to certain individuals among the Manichaeans. Hence, *the Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian report that the Manichaeans reached the very bottom of wicked depravity,* as seen in *Book V of the Code concerning Heretics and Samaritans* and the *Formula for the Reception of Manichaeans* found in Tollius (in the place cited above, page 148).

Regarding the Holy Scripture, they determined that *the God who gave the law through Moses, and who spoke through the Hebrew Prophets, was not the true God, but one of the princes of darkness.* <note>A core Gnostic and Manichaean belief: they viewed the Old Testament God (Yahweh) as an evil or ignorant demiurge, distinct from the benevolent Father of Christ.</note> They read the scriptures of the New Testament as if they were falsified, in such a way that they accept from them whatever they want and reject what they do not want. Because they consider these books as not containing the whole truth, they prefer certain apocryphal writings instead. Regarding the Old Testament, one may consult **EPIPHANIUS** <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a foundational writer on heresies.</note> (page 694 and following); on their invented and forged writings, see both **AUGUSTINE** (Book XXII, chapter 79 of *Against Faustus the Manichaean*) and **TIMOTHEUS**, Presbyter of Constantinople, in his *letter or booklet concerning those who approach the Church* (page 117 of the Meursius edition in *Various Divine Works*), and also the *Formula for the Reception of Manichaeans* (page 142) in Tollius’s *Significant Notes on the Italian Journey with his own commentary.* Regarding the books of **Scythianus** <note>In Christian tradition, Scythianus was a legendary precursor to Mani who supposedly brought dualistic wisdom from Egypt.</note> specifically, which Mani held as the primary sources of his error, see **EPIPHANIUS** (page 629, in the place cited), **CYRIL OF JERUSALEM** (*Catechesis* VI, page 57), and **PHOTIUS** (*Book I, against...*)

...Against the Manichaeans, <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely referring to a work titled *Against the Manichaeans* (Latin: *Contra Manichaeos*).</note> a passage of which may be read from a manuscript hitherto *unpublished* <note>original: *ἀνεκδότῳ*</note> in the celebrated Dr. Fabricius's *Apocryphal Codex of the New Testament*, page 141. But let these points concerning the dogmas of Mani, which sprang from that chief error, suffice. The ancient writers **Epiphanius** and **Augustine** explain these matters more extensively. Augustine was himself once a Manichaean, and therefore all the more worthy of trust, despite the fact that **Becker** <note>Balthasar Bekker (1634–1698), a Dutch minister and author of *The Enchanted World*, who was often criticized for his skeptical views on the supernatural.</note> challenged his credibility with what is certainly a flimsy argument in *The Enchanted World*, Book 1, chapter 18, page 101 of the German edition. The summaries of Titus of Bostra, kindly shared with me by the same [Fabricius], are as follows:

### Summary of the First Discourse

The first discourse contains a refutation and a dismantling of the most essential points of the Manichaean doctrine, showing them to be entirely alien to common natural ideas.

### Summary of the Second Discourse

The second discourse demonstrates that man does not commit sin because of some non-existent, beginningless evil principle that is opposed to God. It shows that nothing among existing things is evil by its very essence, nor is there any inequality in our nature. It argues that they [the Manichaeans] criticize the administration of the universe <note>original: *οἰκονομίαν*, referring to the "divine economy" or the way God manages the world.</note> in vain and with great impiety. It essentially encompasses the entire argument regarding **Providence**, proving that there is no necessity to suspect a second and contrary principle to God based on the nature of things.

### Summary of the third discourse. <note>original Greek: Ὑπόθεσις τοῦ τρίτου λόγου</note>

The third discourse provides a defense of the Law and the Prophets, showing that the entire Old Testament was given by God. It argues that none of the actions or words recorded there offer any reasonable grounds for accusation against the One who acted and spoke. Furthermore, it demonstrates how all these things are in harmony <note>original Greek: σύνοδα, though the author suggests it should read σύνῳδα, meaning "consonant" or "in accord"</note> with the New Testament, so that there is no necessity to suppose a second, opposing principle <note>a reference to the Manichaean belief in two competing gods, one good and one evil</note> against God.

### Summary of the fourth discourse. <note>original Greek: Ὑπόθεσις τοῦ τετάρτου λόγου</note>

The fourth discourse also vindicates the New Testament from their blasphemies against God, showing that they [the Manichaeans] have no true fellowship with it at all. It explains how they vainly attempted to twist certain parts of the New Testament to support their own impiety, and how their arguments regarding the Devil do not assist them in what they claim against God.

In Asia it also infected many in Paphlagonia and the remaining parts of the world.”* 

Thus it is certain that it flourished in Africa during the 4th Century, and that it moved **AUGUSTINE** himself <note>Augustine of Hippo was famously a Manichaean "Hearer" for nine years before converting to Nicene Christianity</note>. However, when this seat of the heretics—and especially Carthage, their metropolis—was fundamentally destroyed and overthrown by **Genseric**, King of the Vandals, they established the seat of their fortunes and dogmas in Italy, and specifically in Rome. 

When this matter reached the ears of Pope **Leo I**, intending to place a sudden barrier against this evil, he held a synod. In this assembly, having summoned the leading figures of the distinguished Senate and the Roman Clergy, and having also gathered the Manichaean Bishops, he exposed their errors, which they displayed in both their doctrine and their way of life, making them abominable to all...

...exposed them as abominable and detestable. From this point on, he <note>Pope Leo I, often called Leo the Great (reigned 440–461 AD)</note> exerted all his intellectual powers to ensure that the followers of Mani would either return to the pure rites of Christ after renouncing their former error, or, if they remained stubborn in their ways, be expelled from the borders of Italy. These events did not take place in 414 AD—which is the opinion of **DANÆUS** <note>Lambert Danaeus, a 16th-century theologian</note> in his notes on *Augustine*, page 226—but rather in the year 444, since Leo only attained his high office in the year 440. See on this matter *Leo I’s Letter 93 to Turibius* and *Sermon 5 on the Fast of the Tenth Month*.

They were betrayed by this specific sign: although they attended the sacred rites of the Christians and received the body of Christ <note>The consecrated bread of the Eucharist</note> along with the others in the Holy Supper <term>Holy Supper|The Eucharist or Communion sacrament</term>, they nevertheless refused to partake of the blood of Christ <note>The sacramental wine. Manichaeans were total abstainers from wine, which they believed to be "the gall of the Prince of Darkness"</note>, as testified by *Leo in Sermon 4 on Lent, page 217*.

Nor was Valentinian III, who at that time ruled the empire with supreme power, remiss in his duty. He provided by law that no Manichaean should be admitted to public office, to bear arms, to give legal testimony, or to ratify contracts. He also prohibited all subjects of his empire from receiving any Manichaean into their homes or concealing one if discovered. Indeed, what may surprise you is that in the *Justinian Code* <note>Latin: *Codex Justinianeus*; the fundamental collection of Roman law</note> Manichaeans are punished by an even more severe law: in Book I, Title V, Law XI, it is ordered that a Manichaean caught in a Roman territory be beheaded. See on this matter **MAIMBURG** <note>Louis Maimbourg, a 17th-century Jesuit historian</note> in his *History of Leo*, page 20 and following, and **BÆLIUS** <note>Pierre Bayle, author of the famous *Historical and Critical Dictionary*</note>, Volume II, page 2027. However, this concern and care, though worthy of praise, did not...

This leader <term>leader|The Latin *antesignanus* literally means a "standard-bearer," or one who stands before the signs in a legion</term> was accustomed to being called sometimes *Seleucus*, sometimes *Leucius*, *Leontius*, *Leuticius*, *Leutius*, or *Lucius*, as has been observed by **CASAUBON** <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar</note> in his *First Exercise against Baronius, no. 15*; **G. J. VOSSIO** in his book *On the Genealogy of Christ, p. 34*; and the celebrated **D. FABRICIUS** in his *Apocryphal Code of the New Testament, p. 137*, and elsewhere. 

He was the corruptor <note>Latin: *interpolator* - one who alters or inserts false material into a text</note> of the *Gospel of the Nativity of Mary*, a fact which **D. FABRICIUS** proves through the testimony of both ancient and modern writers in the previously cited work, pages 3 and following. Regarding these *Seleucians*, **AUGUSTINE** writes in *On Heresies, 59* that they claim the matter of the elements from which the world was made was not created by God, but is co-eternal with God. They also assert that evil originates sometimes from God and sometimes from matter. He links them with the *Hermians*; however, according to the interpretation of **DANÆUS** <note>Lambert Daneau, a 16th-century Calvinist theologian</note> (page 291), this is not to be understood as if they arose at the same time or from the same author, but rather that they adhered to almost the same doctrines. 

Finally, it is established regarding *Leucius* that he attributed false *Acts* to various Apostles—a practice full of deceit, yet one that was surprisingly approved of by the *Manichaeans*. See **D. FABRICIUS**, *Apocryphal Code of the New Testament, p. 768*. The renowned **GRABE** <note>Johannes Ernst Grabe (1666–1711), a scholar of early Christian texts</note> is currently preparing to bring certain fragments and unpublished writings of his to light, as is evident from Volume 1 of his *Spicilegium* <note>Latin: *Spicilegium* - literally a "gleaning" or collection of literary scraps</note>, pages 58 and 78.

### LVII.
Meanwhile, **PRISCILLIAN** in Spain recalled from the underworld <note>original: *ex orco*; referring to the depths of hell</note> the abominable errors of the Gnostics and other heretics, and especially those of the Manichaeans. He omitted nothing that might serve to decorate that "Pandora" <note>A reference to Pandora's box; here used to describe a collection of all possible theological evils and inventions</note> with various myths. **AUGUSTINE**, in his work *On Heresies, 70*, comments on Priscillian's disciples in this way: *“The Priscillianists, whom Priscillian established in Spain, follow a mixture of the dogmas of the Gnostics and the Manichaeans. However, they have also flowed into those depths of filth from other heresies as if into a kind of bilge water <note>original: *sentinam*; a metaphor for a collection of the lowest or most corrupt elements</note> in a horrible state of confusion.”* 

A little further on, the same author continues: *“These people say that souls are of the same nature and substance as God. To engage in a kind of spontaneous struggle on earth, these souls descend through the seven heavens and through certain ranks <term>ranks|The Latin *principatus* refers to celestial powers or principalities in a cosmic hierarchy</term> and run into an evil prince. They claim this world was made by this prince, and that it is sown by him through various works of the flesh.”* 

Compare **SULPICIUS SEVERUS** at the end of his *second book*, who, although he otherwise attributes much to Priscillian and bestows upon him clearly enviable praise for his talent and learning, still bears witness to these errors. He accuses Priscillian and his associates of being guilty of nighttime meetings full of lust. He affirms that Priscillian, having been heard and convicted of sorcery <term>sorcery|The Latin *maleficii* can refer to witchcraft, the occult, or general criminal wrongdoing, which were capital offenses in the Roman legal system</term> by a double judgment, did not deny that he had studied obscene doctrines. Severus further states that he held nighttime gatherings of shameful women and was accustomed to praying while naked, using formal ritualized words <note>original: *conceptis verbis*</note>. Considering these words of Sulpicius, I cannot help but marvel at the impudence of **ARNOLD** <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a controversial church historian known for defending those traditionally labeled as heretics</note>, even though he possesses his own characteristic and in—

**Arnold** <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), whose "impartial" history often sympathized with marginalized groups</note>, indeed, in Part 1, Book 10, Chapter 5, Section 2, page 327, recognizes them also as witnesses to the truth; and while he does not dare to clear them of every crime, he nevertheless thinks that many testimonies were published by them for the truth against the abuses of the **Pontifical Church** <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note>—relying, once again, on no suitable author, which is his usual custom. Afterward it happened that various followers of this heresy chose various seats; indeed, a certain entire group of them is said to have been brought into **France** by a woman named **Hala**. Errors are blamed on her companions, which promoted their condemnation in the **Synod of Orléans** <note>A church council in 1022 which resulted in the first execution for heresy in the medieval West</note>. See **Rodulfus Glaber** <note>An 11th-century chronicler and monk</note>, *History*, Book III, chapter 8.

LX. The **Bogomils** <note>A medieval Gnostic-Manichaean sect that arose in Bulgaria</note> served up the Manichaeans’ "warmed-over cabbage" <note>original: "cramben reco-ctam," a Latin idiom for a tedious repetition</note> yet again, following the example of the **Messalians** <note>Also known as Euchites, a sect that emphasized constant prayer</note>, named after a certain formula frequently repeated in their prayers. See **Sagittarius** <note>Caspar Sagittarianus (1643–1694), a German historian</note>, *Introduction to Church History*, page 891. For if we believe **Euthymius Zigabenus** <note>A 12th-century Byzantine monk and theologian</note> in Title XXIII of the *Panoply* <note>The "Panoplia Dogmatica," a work refuting various heresies</note>, whose words **Lambeck** <note>Peter Lambeck (1628–1680), a librarian and scholar in Vienna</note> in his *Commentary on the Library of Vienna*, Book III, codex 27, page 170, took from a Greek manuscript and...

...left behind, we believe, the name **Bogomil** will signify *one imploring the mercy of God*. His words are these: <note>original Greek: "Βὸγ μεν̀ ἡ τῶν Βουλγάρων γλῶσσα καλεῖ τòν Θεòν, μίλει δὲ τò ἐλέησον. εἴη δ’ ἂν Βογόμιλος κατὰ αὐτοὺς ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ τò ἔλεον ἐπιϲπώμενοϲ."</note> "Bog" is what the Bulgarian language calls God, and "milei" means "have mercy." Thus, according to them, a **Bogomil** would be one who draws down the mercy of God. **Harmenopulus** <note>Constantine Harmenopoulos (c. 1320–1383), a Byzantine jurist and author of a manual on heresies</note> gives the same explanation for the name in his *On the Opinions of Heretics*, Section 19.

Therefore, this dregs of humanity, under a certain leader named **Basil** <note>Basil the Physician, a Bogomil leader who was publicly burned at the stake in the Hippodrome of Constantinople around 1118</note>, raised its head while **Alexios Komnenos** <note>Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos (reigned 1081–1118)</note> held the helm of the empire, and it saw its greatest growth at the beginning of the *12th Century*. Their leader, not trusting in his own talent and distrusting his own deceits, adopted for himself the most filthy fabrications of other heretics; and from the collected filth of the **Manichaeans** and especially the **Messalians** <note>Also known as Euchites or "praying people," an ascetic sect accused of dualism</note>, he finally forged a monstrous heap of opinions. On this matter, **Petau**’s <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a French Jesuit theologian and scholar</note> *On the Incarnation*, Book 15, Chapter 7, Section 5, deserves to be read.

For they differ little from those others regarding the primary head of heavenly doctrine—the creation of the universe—since they assert that **Satan** was indeed created by God and fell through rashness, but they imagine that the world was produced by him, and they acknowledge no other origin for man. To make this more probable and to clothe it with some appearance of truth, they do not hesitate to use various circumstances surrounding the matter—fabricated from their own brains—imagining that the body was first formed from mud, and then the same was provided by God with a vital breath (which the **Devil** could not supply), a fabrication of greater impiety or perhaps stupidity. See **Euthymius** <note>Euthymius Zigabenus, a 12th-century monk commissioned by Emperor Alexios I to refute heresies in his work "The Dogmatic Panoply"</note>, who comments extensively on this matter.

### LXII.

Now we descend to times closer to our own, to investigate whether it is possible to find traces of this same opinion among those who were devoted to the purer sacred rites of Christ <note>This likely refers to the Reformed or Protestant traditions, which the author is contrasting with earlier medieval groups</note>. Indeed, if the *Acts of the Apostles*—falsely attributed to **LEUCIUS** the Manichaean (whom we discussed above)—deserved any credit, this opinion would seem to have been granted citizenship in the Christian community long ago. For **MELLITUS**, Bishop of Laodicea, in the *Passion of St. John the Evangelist* (inserted by **FLORENTINI** in his notes on the edition of the *Martyrology of Jerome*, page 130), recorded these things regarding Leucius, the compiler of those *Acts*:

> "He spoke some truths," he says, "concerning the miracles <note>original: *virtutibus*; literally 'powers,' but used here to mean the miraculous deeds of the Apostles</note> which the Lord performed through them (the Apostles), but concerning doctrine he lied about many things. <meta>This page continues the sentence from the previous page, which quoted the Formula of Concord rejecting the idea that Original Sin is the "substance" of human nature. The author is now identifying the specific theologians (the Flacians) who held this controversial view.</meta>

...for they, just like the Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religious movement that taught the physical world and human bodies were inherently evil and created by a dark power</note> of old, did not distinguish original sin from the very substance of man. They taught that after the Fall, humans were essentially changed from the image of God into the image of the Devil, and thus were the work of the Devil himself. See **Flacius’s** <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a Lutheran reformer who famously argued that original sin was not just a quality, but the very "essence" of fallen man</note> *Key to Holy Scripture*, Part II, Treatise VI, and elsewhere throughout his works, as well as in the book *Know Thyself*. 

From this, **G. J. Vossius** <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a prolific Dutch scholar and theologian</note> says in his *Fragment on the Manichaeans*, Volume VI of his *Collected Works*, page 836: *The association of Flacius Illyricus with the Manichaeans was greater [than others] because, with the exception of only Chapter VI (which concerns an eternal principle of evil), he admits and defends all their other points. Indeed, he maintains along with the Manichaeans that the very substance of man is evil—which God did not make—and that this substance is the cause of all sins. The difference, however, lies in this: the Manichaeans held that human substance was always evil, and that from a beginning that was co-eternal with God; but Illyricus held that the matter was first created good by God, but that the Devil corrupted it,* etc. 

On the differing principles of the Manichaeans and the Flacians, who otherwise agree on almost the same opinion, one should consult among our own writers: **Hutter** <note>Leonhard Hutter (1563–1616), a champion of Lutheran orthodoxy</note> in his *Commentary on the Formula of Concord*, folio 26; **Kromayer** <note>Hieronymus Kromayer (1610–1670), a Lutheran systematic theologian</note> in his *Positive-Polemical Theology*, page 440; and **Dr. Pappus** <note>Johannes Pappus (1549–1610), a Lutheran theologian in Strasbourg</note> in his *Summary of Church History*, page 380. 

Then, he says, *regarding the doctrine of Original Sin itself, this is the difference between the ancient Manichaeans and these recent figures: the former made sin and its author co-eternal with God, and they did not concede that sin arose from a transgression—neither of which our own [the Flacians] wish to be seen affirming.* Compare those who have commented on this error in more detail— <note>original: "men-" — the catchword for the following page, likely "mentions" or "commented"</note>

Thus, the same thing happened here which is almost a common habit among sectarians: they desert their leader himself, and having turned aside with him from the **royal road** <note>A traditional metaphor for the balanced path of orthodox Christian doctrine</note>, they are finally led entirely into the wilderness without him. 

Indeed, what you might find surprising is that the **Flacian** sectarians eventually reached such a height of audacity that they shamelessly—rather than boldly—claimed they could safely catch the arrows of their adversaries by using the **Book of Concord** <note>The foundational collection of Lutheran doctrinal documents published in 1580</note> itself as a shield. LXIV. **EILHARD LUBIN** <note>Eilhard Lubin (1565–1621), a German philosopher and theologian at the University of Rostock</note> comes closer to this **Manichaean** decree. He was initially a professor of humanities and later a public Doctor of Theology at **Rostock**. Because he was not sufficiently learned in the precepts of **Philosophy** nor nurtured in them, he attempted a completely new way of demonstrating the origin of sin, though it was an unhappy effort. He published a unique book in **Rostock** in the year 1596, which was reprinted there in 1600 in octavo and duodecimo formats under the title: *Phosphorus <note>original: "Phosphori"; the title refers to the "Morning Star" or "Light-Bringer," suggesting a work that clarifies a dark subject</note>, or a Hypermetaphysical Treatise on the First Cause and Nature of Evil*, in which the most serious disputes of many are removed and errors are detected. His opinion comes down to this: that there are two co-eternal principles, namely **God** as the principle of Good and **Nothingness** <note>original: "Nihilum"</note> as the principle of evil. Therefore, thinking that the nature of sin is fulfilled by an inclination toward **Nothingness**, he established that sin was necessary so that the Nature of good might be perceived and known. Thus, he attributed to this "nothing" all those things which **Aristotle** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose works on "prime matter" were central to medieval and early modern science</note> taught regarding his own "first nature" <note>original: "natura sua prima"; referring to Aristotle's concept of prime matter, which has no qualities of its own but can receive them</note>. His words are clear, and entirely worthy of being repeated here to perceive his mind:

*If anyone asks me,* he says, *who made evil? I will truly respond, Nothing made evil. If anyone asks: what is Evil? I will rightly respond: Evil is Nothing. If you demand a reason, I will give it, because, as is established among all,*

They say, however, that this internal man is not stained or infected even if the external man is struggling with the very worst filth of life. **Thomas Aquinas** <note>original: *Thomas*; referring to *Summa Theologica* I-II, Question 82, Article 3.</note> and others say that original sin is a certain "corrupted habit" <note>In medieval philosophy, a "habit" refers to a settled disposition or tendency of the soul.</note>. **Robert Bellarmine** <note>A prominent Jesuit Cardinal and Counter-Reformation theologian.</note> admits that this is also the opinion of **Gregory of Rimini**, **Henry of Ghent**, and **Johannes Driedo**; namely, that it is a certain diseased quality in the soul that constantly stirs up wicked desires. One can easily judge from these facts whether the Scholastics—and the Catholics and **Innovators** <note>original: *Novatores*; usually a pejorative term for those introducing new theological ideas, often referring to Pietists or followers of Georg Calixtus.</note> who followed them—do not truly join the side of the Manichaeans. By inventing a "state of pure Naturals" <note>original: *statu merorum Naturalium*; a theological concept describing humanity as possessing only natural powers without divine grace.</note>, they place two entirely separate principles within man. The Great Man opposed this fiction in his *System, Volume IV, on the State of Integrity, Question 1, page 467*, and in his *Harmony of Calixtine-Heresy, page 217*. Indeed, they may even seem worse than the Manichaeans because they make **God the author of sin**, since they believe man was placed in that "state of pure Naturals" by God.

**LXX.** The cohort of **Calvinists** <note>Followers of John Calvin.</note>, having avoided this extreme (in which those who have fallen away add a new God to God), swerve into the opposite extreme, and pronounce God Himself to be the author of sin. I am certainly not unaware...

**TURRETINUS** <note>original: "TUS"; referring to Francis Turretin (1623–1687), a highly influential Genevan Reformed theologian known for his "Institutes of Elenctic Theology."</note>, Professor at Geneva, did not guard himself from the same error, to the point that he involved himself in even greater darkness? ## SECTION III.

### Demonstrating the falsity of the opinion regarding two Principles.

->§. I.<-

Having completed the first two sections and being about to enter upon the third, we shall strive to place the falseness <note>original: "vanitatem"</note> of this opinion in a clearer light. We do so all the more because that universal agreement and conspiracy of impious minds in asserting this hypothesis seems to grant it a not insignificant appearance of truth. It will not be a task of great labor to complete this business if we attack that persuasion with reason alone; however, we may perhaps experience greater difficulty if we take it upon ourselves to defend our own view against the battering rams <note>original: "arietibus"; a metaphor for the heavy logical attacks of opponents.</note> of our adversaries. 

Moreover, it is established by various arguments from the nature of things that it is impossible for there to be two **co-eternal Beings** <term>co-eternal Beings: The concept that two separate entities, such as a Good God and an Evil God (or God and Matter), have both existed forever without a beginning.</term> of equal power, devoted to entirely different pursuits and leaning toward opposite directions. <meta>This page continues the critique of Manichaean dualism. While the previous page argued that a God who loses parts of himself to evil is unwise and incomplete, this page explores the logical "trap" these thinkers fall into: in trying to protect God's reputation from being the "source of evil," they inadvertently describe a God who is either powerless or cruel for allowing his creations to be tortured by an external enemy.</meta>

(317)

Fleeing from calling Him the cause of evil, they describe Him as utterly evil; and, according to the proverb, "fleeing the smoke, they have fallen into the fire." Therefore, this reasoning is impious regarding the divine. <note>original Greek: Φεύγοντες αἴτιον αὐτὸν τοῦ κακοῦ εἰπεῖν, πάγκα- κον ὑπογράφουσι καὶ κατὰ τὴν παροιμίαν φεύγον- τες τὸν καπνὸν εἰς πῦρ ἐμπεπτώκασι. οὕτω μὲν οὖν ἀσεβὴς περὶ τὸ θεῖον οὗτος ὁ λόγος.</note> That is: *And so, while they refuse to call God the cause of evil, they describe evil as being present in every part [of the divine]: and as the proverb says, fleeing the smoke, they fell into the fire. Therefore, this reasoning is impious toward God, etc.* <note>original Latin: itaque dum mali causam dicere Deum recusant, ab omni parte malum describunt: & ut proverbio dicitur, fumum fugientes in ignem inciderunt. Ideo igitur & impia adversus Deum est ista ratio &c.</note> The same point was seen by **WILLIAM KING**, Bishop of Derry, in his book *On the Origin of Evil*, chapter II, page 49 and following. For he, intending to show that the difficulties pressing upon any discussion of the origin of evil are not removed by the <term>Manichaean hypothesis</term> <note>The belief that the universe is a battlefield between two equal powers: a Good God and an Evil Principle</note>, argues as follows:

*He who knowingly creates something destined to be afflicted with misery by another is no less to be blamed than if he had created something he foresaw would bring misery upon itself. If, therefore, God’s goodness could remain intact while creating things He knew a "Bad Principle" could and would corrupt (as the Manichaeans asserted), then that same goodness could remain intact even if He created things that would corrupt themselves or perish over the course of time. If, according to the supporters of this view, God ought to have refrained from creating those things in which malice or opposition were inherent, He ought also to have refrained from creating those whose natures He foresaw the Bad Principle would ruin. And if there was so much goodness in those things that He judged it better to create them—even if they were eventually to be corrupted by an enemy power—He could just as easily have judged it better to bring them into being even if they were eventually to perish from their own internal flaws.*

I have undertaken this entire dissertation against the Manichaeans following the lead of **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century philosopher and one of the last great Neoplatonists; he was a "gentile" (pagan) who used logic to critique the dualist systems of his time</note>, so that their lack of foresight might be made even more manifest when subjected to the judgment of a pagan philosopher—

<meta>This page continues the logical critique of Manichaean dualism, specifically addressing the philosophical impossibility of having two equal, opposing "First Principles" (Good and Evil). It references the skepticism of Pierre Bayle and the Neoplatonic arguments of Simplicius to show that logic requires a single "One" to exist before any "Many."</meta>

(318)

<note>The sentence completes from the previous page:</note> ...would be stripped of every appearance of truth. Indeed, I do not doubt that this argument satisfies everyone and easily proves its own character and learning: although regarding the first reasoning, which stands in the front line of the debate, it may seem more subtle than true to **BAYLE** <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a famous French philosopher and skeptic known for his *Historical and Critical Dictionary*.</note> on page 3150. The whole matter comes down to this: these principles are said to be contraries, but such things cannot exist unless they are included under some common <term>genus</term> <note>In logic, a 'genus' is a broad category that contains sub-categories or 'species'. For example, 'Color' is a genus, while 'Black' and 'White' are contrary species within it.</note>; otherwise, they would hold the status of being merely different things, not contraries. It is necessary, therefore, to establish another principle that is prior to and higher than both of them, and this alone, in the end, deserves the name of "First Principle," nor can any other easily share in that name. The words are expressed thus:

> For different things are not simply contraries. For this reason, it is also impossible for contraries to be principles, because it is necessary for a common category to exist before them; and furthermore, because it is necessary for the One to exist before the many. <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ τὰ διάφορα ἁπλῶς ἐναντία ἐστί. - Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἀδύνατον τὰ ἐναντία ἀρχὰς εἶναι, ὅτι ἀνάγκη προυπάρχειν αὐτῶν τὸ κοινὸν γένος, καὶ μέντοι καὶ διότι ἀνάγκη πρὸ πλήθους τὸ ἕν εἶναι.</note>

Indeed, **BAYLE** thinks that little weight should be given to this argument on the grounds that it rests upon the slippery foundation of <term>genus and species</term>, which he claims are merely fictions and notions of the mind. But in truth, since the learned man would willingly and not reluctantly grant that <term>ideas</term> are adapted to the nature of things, and are not entirely destitute of any foundation, **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle and a famous refutation of Manichaean dualism.</note>, among others, took it upon himself to defend this cause.

<meta>This page continues the critique of the Manichaean hypothesis regarding the origin of evil. Having established on the previous page that logic requires a single "First Principle," the author now explores the moral and ethical consequences of believing in an independent, powerful Principle of Evil that compels human behavior.</meta>

(319)

He shows that this same hypothesis is entangled in absurdities. For he wisely foresaw, and no less diligently exposed, that the entire foundation of Ethics is undermined by this hypothesis as if by a battering ram; he saw that shackles are cast upon free will and reins applied, and finally that all religion and worship of the Deity is abolished. 

For he argues in this way: a Principle of Evil is introduced by Philosophers of this kind as something exceedingly powerful, by which souls—no longer left in their own power—are stirred and compelled to commit atrocities. From this, it certainly follows that a person, since they sin against their will, does not truly transgress at all, and thus deserves an excuse and pardon for their vices. 

Who does not see that in this way all evil is abolished? And who fails to notice that the very "principle of evil" is uprooted by this logic? For since they have introduced this Principle as the cause of evils, but these [evils] turn out to be non-existent <note>The author argues that if a "sin" is forced, it isn't a moral evil or a true sin, so "evil" as a moral category disappears.</note>, it follows that the Principle itself collapses. If the effect of a cause that is supposedly always in action is removed, the cause itself must necessarily vanish into smoke. 

The words are worthy of being read in the Greek language, the meaning of which I have expressed here in English:

> He destroys the principles of moral guidance <note>original Greek: Φυσικῆς ἐυαγωγίας - literally 'natural guidance' or 'ethical training'.</note> as far as he is able, by truly abolishing what is "up to us" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν - a technical philosophical term referring to human agency or things within our own power.</note>; for he introduces the principle of evil as unbegotten, indestructible, and powerful, pushing souls by force into evil.

And so the matter is led to the point where neither are these "favorable" nor are those "unfavorable," or—which is impossible—both are themselves favorable, and both are again unfavorable.

VIII. Since we have now ourselves attacked the false opinion of our adversaries, it would be entirely fair for us to also grant them the opportunity to bring their own arguments into the open. For a complete system requires not only that it be built upon firm foundations, but also that it not be easily exposed to the battering rams of others—attacks that might cause the entire structure to wobble and threaten it with ruin. > *No truth*, he says, *is inconvenient when nothing is believed, and everything is doubted.*

This will be easily judged by anyone who observes that God's plans in building the structure of this universe were directed not only toward providing a proof of His goodness, but also toward making His glory manifest to men—a glory which shines forth no less in the other attributes of the Divine Power than in His goodness. For not only does sound reason teach that all things were created primarily for the glory of God, but Scripture further confirms this in Proverbs 16:4 <note>"The Lord hath made all things for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil."</note>. The meaning of this thesis is not that God, in constructing the world, strove for His own glory in the same way that men—who, when left to themselves, are creatures driven by vanity <note>original: *gloriae animalcula*; literally "little animals of glory," a disparaging term for humans who seek fame.</note>—direct most or even all of their actions toward hunting for some shadow of praise. 

Far be it from us to think of God in such a way, for He is most far removed from this impure emotion; rather, He is said to have created all things for His glory in the sense that He brought to light not only His goodness, but all His other attributes, and especially His wisdom. **William King** <note>William King (1650–1729) was the Archbishop of Dublin and author of *De Origine Mali* (1702), a key work defending divine providence against skepticism.</note> rightly noted this in *On the Origin of Evil*, Chapter 1, Section 10, page 44. Therefore, when Scripture teaches us that the world was created for the glory of God, it must be understood that the divine attributes—namely, power, goodness, and wisdom—shine so clearly in His works..."

XIII. We observed previously that those theologians who hold a "middle path" here do not at all establish reason as contrary to revelation—or Philosophy as contrary to Theology—but only as inferior. Thus, while there are many dogmas of faith that they cannot reach through human thought alone, once these are established, many of these thinkers are occupied in demonstrating that reason generally accords well with Scripture in many places. 

But **BAYLE’S** opinion is different; he thinks that reason is always opposed to faith. He believes that reason not only does nothing to confirm the articles of faith, but is also powerless to defend them against the objections of unbelievers. ...[that the whole] is more perfect than a part; this is evident from the fact that it necessarily possesses the manifold perfection of each individual part. Moreover, when parts are joined and connected to one another, they acquire a specific and new perfection, by virtue of which they serve their own ends—ends for which they would be unsuitable individually—and they better offer mutual aid and defend themselves. 

Just as, therefore, either a house or a clock does not consist of parts that are equal in every respect or of the same value and labor, but of such parts as are sometimes of lesser and sometimes of greater importance—and yet each individual part belongs to and is required for the completion of the entire structure and machine—so too does reason, even when left to itself (provided it is sober), judge that the **world-machine** <term>world-machine</term> <note>original: *mundi machinam*; a common philosophical metaphor in the 17th and 18th centuries likening the universe to a complex, designed mechanism like a clock.</note> is likewise arranged. And if reason detects any imperfections in the parts, it ascribes them not to the weakness of the **Creator** <note>original: *Conditoris*; literally "the Founder" or "the Builder."</note> but to the nature and finite condition of the whole, enclosed within its own limits. 

Thus, just as it is the mark of a wise craftsman to take no less account of the minor parts than of the larger and more excellent ones—since otherwise he would have to abandon the plan of forming the work altogether—so it is fitting to admire and call infinite both the wisdom and the goodness of God. For He omitted not even the slightest thing that was possible to be made (even though He could have produced far more), but instead contributed everything toward the perfection of the entire work, to be finished in every detail <note>original: *omnibus numeris absolvendam*; a Latin idiom meaning "perfected in all respects" or "complete in every part."</note>.

*...if it would have been best, He would have done it without a doubt. For it was fitting for Him not to omit even the smallest thing that could possibly be made. **Finite goodness** could be exhausted by creating only greater things, but **infinite goodness** extends itself to all things. Therefore, the fact that imperfect things exist alongside more perfect ones is caused by infinite and divine goodness.* I add that it is a greatest argument for the infinite goodness of God that God founded man, even though He prudently knew that man—disregarding the reasons for a grateful spirit—would later be less than obedient to the laws He had established. 

Thinking, therefore, that the case for divine goodness in the creation of **imperfect Beings** <term>imperfect Beings</term> <note>original: *Entium imperfectorum*; in philosophy, "beings" or "entities" that are limited or lacking the full perfection of the Creator.</note> has been abundantly argued and vindicated, I will mention in the final place that the cited assertion of **Bayle** <note>original: *Baelii*; referring to Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a hugely influential French philosopher whose skeptical arguments about the existence of evil often challenged traditional religious views.</note>, in which God is said to have been obliged to confer infinite perfections upon His creatures, can pull the minds of men like a torrent into the unfortunate whirlpool of **Atheism**, although I would not rashly dare to affirm that he put it forward with that intention. 

For since we see that various creatures have been produced in this universe as imperfect in various ways—not only when they are compared with God, but even when compared with things of their own kind—we must either grant that they could be created with such inequality, or, if we stubbornly deny this, we must by the same effort deny that creatures draw their origin from anyone at all. Who is there who does not know that this contains the seeds of **Atheism**?

Once the reasons for **free will** <term>free choice</term> <note>original: *liberi arbitrii*; the theological and philosophical concept that humans can choose between different courses of action without divine or natural compulsion.</note> have been laid out, we will easily grant to **Bayle** <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a famous French philosopher and skeptic known for his *Historical and Critical Dictionary*, which often highlighted the tensions between human reason and religious faith.</note> that those arguments he thought could be brought forward are neither valid nor suitable. But who is there who does not understand that the logic between these two compared things is very different? For the mother, in this imagined scenario, certainly cannot be certain whether the daughter (whom she foresees will suffer corruption) has been previously nourished with such honorable morals and teachings that she might be able to resist the corruption when it is offered; thus, the mother makes herself a party to recklessness and crime by subjecting her daughter to such a great danger, which she even foresees.

But truly, God knew that man was equipped with all the means necessary for him to maintain a true and upright use of **free will**. Thus, He did nothing contrary to His own goodness while permitting man, so established, to exercise this freedom. Furthermore, a mother has received a command to see to the protection of her daughter's integrity; if she neglects this, she would be guilty of disobedience and neglect of duty. Who, indeed, can assert anything similar regarding God?

Moreover, a mother can provide no remedy for the evil that arises from that exposure of her daughter that could repair the loss already suffered. Regarding God, however, we human beings are persuaded otherwise, convinced by certain proofs of reality concerning the sincere **will of God** <term>will of God</term> <note>original: *voluntas Dei*; refers to the divine desire for human salvation and righteousness.</note> and His most full **power** <term>power</term> <note>original: *potestas*.</note> to restore humans to wholeness <note>The text cuts off here at the word *integrum* (wholeness/integrity), likely leading into a discussion of divine redemption or restoration after the Fall.</note>

This is established by these principles: that God, because of the extremely close union of the soul with the body, forms certain ideas in the soul upon the presence of certain physical movements; and conversely, He produces certain movements in the body upon the presence of certain acts of the will. 

From this, it follows by an easy consequence that man can be considered the author of absolutely no action—whether the soul or the body had the greater part in performing it—since each part of man provides only the "occasion" for God to exercise His power in man and to work through him as if through some kind of instrument. Bayle, among others, holds this conviction, although he clearly perceives that it is extremely injurious to human freedom.

### XXII.

Before we assert the **liberty of choice** in man, we believe it will be worth our while to recall Bayle’s cited reasons for examination. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between divine causality and human agency. Following the critique of François Lami's occasionalism—which suggests God is the sole cause of all sensations—the text now addresses the distinction between God providing the "power" to act and the human "determination" of the act itself.</meta>

<page-num>(418)</page-num>

...[the power of] acting <note>The Latin fragment "randi" is the end of a word like "operandi" (acting) from the previous page.</note> by obtaining these strengths from God throughout the entire span of life is, in a way, to be created; for, without these strengths, the creature would fall back into its original nothingness. Thus, no small flaw in the argument would be committed if we were to assert that it is not the human who uses these granted strengths, but God himself who uses them to produce whatever actions occur. 

In the same way, a King can grant to a subject the free power to exercise a certain office; as long as the subject performs those duties, he is to be considered appointed to that task by the King. But if it should happen that the administrator of the office abuses his power, having no regard for the laws prescribed by the King, would anyone drag the King into a partnership in that abuse? Or would anyone bring a legal charge against the King for neglected duties simply because he supplied the man with the strength and the faculty to act? 

The logic of this matter is the same when we call the preservation of creatures by the name of **continued creation** <note>The philosophical concept that God does not just create the world once, but must actively "re-create" or sustain it at every moment to prevent it from vanishing.</note>. This is because creatures depend on God for both their existence and their operation, but in such a way that they themselves must be judged to act freely. I believe my thought should be expressed in the words of the late **SCHERZER** <note>Johann Adam Scherzer (1628–1689), a Lutheran theologian and philosopher known for his work on divine providence and the soul.</note>. In his *System of Providence*, page 132, section 11, he writes:

> From whatever source a thing depends for its existence, it also depends for its acting—specifically regarding the principle (so that it possesses the power of acting in such a way) and its preservation—though not (in the case of free agents) regarding the determination. For a free being, by the very fact that it is free, determines its own free action. <note>original Latin: "A quo quid dependet in esse, ab eo etiam in operari, ratione scilicet principii (ut habeat potentiam taliter operandi) & conservationis, licet non (quoad agentia libera) determinationis. Ens enim liberum hoc ipso, quid liberum est, suam actionem liberam determinat."</note>

I believe it is necessary to bring forward certain arguments to perceive the vanity <note>In this context, "vanity" refers to the futility or lack of logical foundation in the opposing theory.</note> of this position. I say nothing of the fact that manifest experience of things opposes this, and that those **phenomena** <note>observable events or facts</note> are observed by us daily, the account for which the patron of these principles will not be allowed to give.

For what, I ask, is the cause why some actions can be performed by us with easy effort and are actually performed, while all others exceed our powers, even if we are carried away by the greatest desire to produce them? What is the reason why God—having excited this will to act in my mind—does not then also produce those movements in the body which satisfy the soul's desire? Thus, a weight of lighter mass can be lifted and raised by a man of thin strength, but that same man will not move a grander mass even a fingernail's breadth. ### XXV.

Having thus undermined the reasons for disagreement offered by Bayle regarding human freedom, we shall now direct our effort and study toward briefly building up that very case. In this, however, it must be held from the start—as we have already warned above—that we are arguing the cause of freedom not at all in the theological forum, but in the philosophical one. We establish that man possesses **free will** only in external, moral, and civil actions, which are measured against the standard of either virtue or vice. 

The Papal doctors <note>Roman Catholic theologians</note> of our sacred matters, either neglecting or concealing this distinction, have wrongly included us among the number of those who would strip all freedom from the human will. On our part, however, we must especially take account of this distinction, lest an occasion be provided to Bayle or any other person to rashly change the <term>matter at issue<note>original Greek: τὸ κρινόμενον (to krinomenon)</note></term>, or the state of the controversy...

By the power of **free will** <note>original: *liberæ voluntatis*</note>, we know ourselves to be the true authors of our actions; in turn, we grieve over things done badly, but not over all of them. Rather, we grieve for those things which we see we could have avoided by the right use of our **choice** <term>arbitrium: the capacity of the mind to decide between different courses of action</term>. For the most part, however, we are indifferent, or at least we are not so touched by grief over those things which did not happen through our own fault, even though we understand them to be either less than right or harmful to our **happiness** <note>original: *felicitati*</note>. 

For this reason, the **teachers of morals** <term>morum Doctores: a general term for philosophers or theologians who specialize in ethics</term> have demonstrated, not only with arguments but also with various examples, that we should grieve either not at all or only very slightly over those adversities of fortune which come upon us undeservedly. However, they argue that a different account must be taken of those which we seem to have brought upon ourselves through either imprudence or stubbornness. Nor will anyone judge otherwise who has more accurately examined the inner compartments <note>original: *forulos*—literally "little boxes" or "pigeon-holes," a metaphor for the secret recesses of the mind</note> of his own mind. 

Hence, it is no wonder that the power of **conscience** <note>original: *conscientiæ*</note> in human affairs is so great that those who are driven by its terrors consider themselves the most miserable of all, and would rather suffer the loss of life itself than remain subject to its tyranny. Is it at all likely that men devoted to wickedness would not relieve themselves of this most heavy burden, if it were somehow possible and if the whole matter rested on a vain persuasion? For who will allow himself to be persuaded to suffer the most exquisite pains from the memory of a thing for which he does not believe himself to be the true author, and concerning which he is convinced that, in performing it, he followed the will of another <note>original: *alienæ*</note> rather than his own?

He himself acknowledges that his own position is hard-pressed on page 160. <meta>This page continues the critique of Archbishop William King’s "De Origine Mali" (On the Origin of Evil), specifically addressing the "Highest Good" and how it relates to the human will. The previous page discussed whether the faculty of the will acts blindly or follows the intellect.</meta>

<meta>catchword: ple- [likely: complectitur, meaning "includes"]</meta>

The **Learned Man** <note>Referring to William King</note> had trusted that, up until now, it has not been explained what sort of **Highest Good** <term>Highest Good: In philosophy, the *Summum Bonum*, or the ultimate goal and value that provides the basis for all moral actions</term> should be held in the highest place and value. For he himself has not set forth what the objects are toward which that **free power** <note>the will</note> is primarily carried by its own motion. Furthermore, I do not see what disadvantage affects or burdens this opinion, since the **liberty** of the **will** <term>will: the faculty of choosing or deciding</term> remains constant regardless; nor should he struggle much if he were ignorant of it, because if he ever finds it, he cannot help but be drawn and led toward it. 

Regarding the matter itself, I would not deny that this controversy was debated with great mental effort by the ancient philosophers, who went in different directions, not being very consistent with themselves, as appears from **CICERO’S** very elegant books *On the Ends of Good and Evil* <note>original: *de Finibus*</note> and **MALLINCROT’S** <note>Bernard von Mallinckrodt (1591–1664), a German scholar who wrote on the Highest Good</note> commentary *On the Highest Good* <note>original: *de Summo Bono*</note>. Meanwhile, this case has not been left entirely undecided or **still before the judge** <note>original: *sub judice*; a legal term meaning a case is still under consideration</note>, since at least most of the ancients agreed that the **Highest Good** should be placed either in **tranquility of the mind** or in **assimilation with God**, which the **Platonists** as well as the **Pythagoreans** and many others yearned for. Regarding the moderns, there is no room for doubt that most, if not almost all, believe God should be held in the place of the Highest Good, and they judge correctly. Therefore, there is nothing here that **KING** <note>Archbishop William King</note> could rightly demand. Specifically, his argument is that if the **will** can suspend an act which the **intellect** <term>intellect: the faculty of reasoning and understanding, distinct from the will or the emotions</term> has persuaded it to undertake, it follows entirely that the **will** can be carried toward **evil**.

1. Firstly, part of this must be attributed to the **intellect** when it does not perceive a thing correctly.
2. Secondly, part must be attributed to the **will**, which often—as we saw above—as it were forces or at least impels the **intellect** to hold something in the place of **good**. Without the impulse of the **will**, that object would hardly seem good at all. 

Regarding **choices** <term>choices: original *electionibus*, refers to the act of picking one thing over another</term> of the first kind—those caused by simple misunderstanding—a person is not usually very anxious or prone to feel great sorrow and sickness. However, he is distressed much more vehemently by the latter kind, since he knows those choices were contracted by his own fault and vice.

### XXXIV.

Thus far, King has argued only from his established premises, while he supposed that such a **free power** could be conceived which would be determined solely by itself, with no consideration given to the nature of things themselves. Now he proceeds further and attempts to demonstrate that a **Being** <term>Being: *Ens*, an existing entity</term> endowed with this power actually exists, and for this purpose, he appeals to **God**. For he judges that, for Him, nothing was externally good or evil before His choice, but rather He established His will alone as the cause of goodness in creatures, which was by no means determined by the goodness of the things created. Here, indeed, the Learned Man will find us easily in agreement: that there was nothing outside of God by which He might be [moved] to fashion certain creatures...
