Now, therefore, we must discuss what sort of divine concepts these might be. I believe no one will doubt that they always correspond to the holiness, goodness, justice, and other attributes of the **Supreme Name** <note>original: *Summi Nominis*; a respectful way to refer to God</note>. If they do so correspond, it cannot be otherwise than that the things themselves—having been fashioned after the pattern of those ideas—are so constituted that they carry with them the traces of those attributes.

Since no thing is deprived of its own properties, it must be exactly as the **Creator** <note>original: *opifex*; literally "craftsman" or "artificer"</note> and Master willed it to be. Moreover, He could not have willed it to be otherwise than as His own essence and constitution suggests. Therefore, since God the Creator is supremely holy, supremely good, and likewise supremely just, it would seem an injustice to each of these attributes for someone not to see at least a shadow of them in the creatures themselves, or not to be able to reach a knowledge of those attributes through them.

**KING** <note>William King (1650–1729)</note> saw this, yet he partially pretended not to see it when he wrote on page 156: *“It is certain that the divine will had both His goodness and His wisdom as companions here, as in all things; but it is from the will immediately that things please God, that is...”* <note>original: *Certum voluntatem divinam, tam bonitatem quam sapientiam ejus hic ut in omnibus comites habuisse...*</note>

This variety ensures that a single drop, possessing its own distinct particles, changes the liquid's texture and thus equips it with new qualities. 

I do not wish to be too wordy on these matters, regarding which more ample evidence from the treasures of nature will be supplied by **Robert Boyle** <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691) was a founding figure of modern chemistry and a pioneer of the scientific method.</note>—that most excellent English **initiate into nature’s mysteries** <note>original: "naturæ mysta" — a term of high respect, suggesting Boyle is like a priest who understands the secret workings of the natural world.</note>—in his book *On the Origin of Forms and Qualities*, and by **Jean Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736) was a prominent scholar whose "Physica" was a widely used textbook on natural philosophy.</note> in his *Physics*, Book 5, Chapter 6, page 389.

This motion depends on the diversity of the texture, either of the objects themselves or of our own **organs of sense** <note>the eyes, ears, nose, etc.</note>, whether the sensation we perceive is one of pleasure or of pain. 

Whether, therefore, a pleasant scent is carried to our nostrils, or the touch perceives a delightful sensation, or the taste is affected by a singular pleasure—or if the opposites of all these occur—the cause should be sought nowhere else than in the varied disposition of matter. For it is impossible that if one specific motion of matter gives rise to a pleasant and agreeable sensation, another motion, which is contrary to it, would not also be the source of a contrary effect. ### XXXIX.
Finally, we must not omit that argument which a certain class of complaining people—dissatisfied with their lot—is accustomed to use to attack God's goodness. This argument is drawn both from wild animals and from poisons, which they convince themselves were created only for the destruction of the human race.

Therefore, as far as wild animals are concerned, we are taught daily that they themselves provide no small utility to human affairs. If this utility were weighed against the harms that usually reach us from them, it would be, in my judgment, doubtful to which side the advantage should be ascribed. Furthermore, the harms and inconveniences that humans perceive from them are not so great or so numerous, since rare examples are given of those who have experienced the fury <term>rabies - here meaning wild ferocity or madness</term> of wild beasts to the detriment of their life and health. Certainly, most of those who happen to perish in such a way must necessarily attribute it to their own fault, rashness, or negligence. I will not mention that humans, by divine favor, have discovered many ways by which they might either guard themselves from the injuries of wild beasts, or [tame] them...

For although He had to grant opposing motions to matter (unless He wished for there to be no motion at all), He nevertheless provided both certain signs and the most immediate remedies so that the evils arising from them could either be removed as they attacked or avoided while they were still imminent.

### XL.
Now we shall hear what **Bayle** <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706) was a French philosopher whose *Historical and Critical Dictionary* famously explored the problem of evil and skepticism.</note> brought against these points in his attempt to respond to **King** <note>William King (1650–1729), the Archbishop of Dublin, wrote *De Origine Mali* (On the Origin of Evil), arguing that physical evils are necessary consequences of the nature of matter.</note> in the passage cited above. Indeed, it was observed earlier that, in **Bayle's** own judgment, this thesis—which derives **physical evils** <term>physical evil: suffering or harm caused by natural processes, such as pain, disease, or disasters, rather than by human sin.</term> from the condition of matter—could put the "finishing stroke" <note>original: *colophonem imponere* — a traditional metaphor meaning to complete or perfect an argument.</note> to this entire controversy; yet, he thinks it wise to deny that thesis entirely. Lest I be long-winded, I will provide his words translated into English <note>The original manuscript provides these words translated from Bayle’s French into Latin; they are rendered here into English for the reader.</note>:

> *The worst part,* he says, *is that our reason finds no logical necessity here. However, reason does not sufficiently perceive that there is a necessary connection between certain motions of bodies and the unpleasant sensations of heat or cold, hunger or thirst, pain and sadness. Therefore, reason judges that this connection was established by a **Free Being** <note>original: *Ente libero* — referring to God as a creator acting with free will rather than by blind necessity.</note>, who could not have acted in such a way according to the example of a **Good Principle** <note>original: *Boni Principii* — a reference to the concept of a purely benevolent deity, often contrasted with an "evil principle" in Manichaean or dualist philosophy.</note>, and thus it [reason] requires an explanation...*

It is manifest that people are of this mind because many, when asked why they so greatly prefer life and place it above all other things, will not only offer the pleasantness of living as a pretext, but will point to one or two specific reasons that stir this desire in their souls. 

Hence, those who either complain excessively about life or take the counsel to throw it away usually condemn their own imprudence <term>imprudentia: a lack of foresight or practical wisdom</term> and detest their own neglect of the use of reason <term>ratio: the mental faculty of logic and judgment</term> once they return to themselves—that is, when the intensity of their pain subsides and they enjoy the free power of using their reason again. ### XLII.

But perhaps Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), the skeptic whose arguments the author is refuting.</note> might grant that these things can be reconciled with the goodness of God. For this is contrary both to the judgment of reason and even to the **Holy Scripture** <note>original: "Sacro etiam Codici"</note>, which has left on record the complaints of those to be damned, by which they detest the life they see being painfully prolonged in the midst of fires.

There remains another method, and it was explained by **STILLINGFLEET** <note>Edward Stillingfleet (1635–1699), a prominent Anglican theologian and Bishop of Worcester</note>, formerly a Bishop of the English, in a certain sermon which recently appeared along with others in the English language. This theory consists in the following: that if faith must be held in the sacred <term>Pandects</term> <note>The term "Pandects" usually refers to a complete body of laws; here, it refers to the Bible as the definitive collection of divine law</note>, the endless duration of infernal punishments cannot but be affirmed. However, if reason is too repugnant to this dogma, he thinks it can likewise be believed that these punishments were proclaimed by the Supreme Deity as a kind of threat <note>original: "minarum instar"</note>, so that people might be kept more strictly and correctly in their duty. Meanwhile, it is permitted for God, as the supreme author of the law, to loosen the reins of mercy at whatever time He pleases, and to set a measure and limits to the punishments, if He judges that they cannot consist with His own goodness.

Reviewing this hypothesis, **LE CLERC** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a Genevan theologian and influential scholar</note> in *Volume VIII of the Selected Library* <note>original: "Bibl. Select.", referring to Le Clerc's journal "Bibliothèque Choisie"</note>, professes that his mind is not altogether averse to it. Why indeed should the same judgment not be passed on divine promises—nay, on all other things which, like Oracles <note>original: "Oraculorum instar"; referring to divine pronouncements of absolute truth</note>, ought to be followed with the highest veneration?

Consequently, others have thought it more advisable to return to the nature of infernal punishments, and they suggest that, since that nature is not fully perceived by us, no judgment can be formed about them or their compatibility with divine goodness. For they say perhaps the mere deprivation of the eternal good <note>original: "boni aeterni privationem"; this refers to the "poena damni" or the "punishment of loss"—the pain of being separated from God, as opposed to the "poena sensus" or "punishment of the senses" (physical fire)</note> completes all the punishments of the damned, and thus can easily be reconciled with the goodness of God. **JAQUELOT** <note>Isaac Jaquelot (1647–1708), a French Huguenot theologian who wrote on the harmony of reason and faith</note> does not hesitate to state this in Chapter VII of *The Conformity of Reason and Faith, p. 217*, and **LE CLERC** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Genevan scholar and theologian</note> does not seem far from this view in Volume IX of the *Select Library, p. 142*.

In the meantime, consult the blessed <note>original: "B."; an honorific for deceased theologians</note> **CALOVIUS** <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a leading defender of Lutheran Orthodoxy</note> and **SCHERTZERUS** <note>Johann Adam Schertzer (1628–1683), a Lutheran theologian known for his polemics against heresy</note>, who have disputed this cause extensively and solidly in their anti-Socinian <note>The Socinians were a sect that rejected the Trinity and often the eternity of hell</note> writings, such that I consider them to have spared me the trouble of further work. Let the complete treatise of **Dr. FECHTIUS** <note>Johannes Fecht (1636–1716)</note> be added, published in 1683 under the title *Consideration of the State of the Damned, regarding specifically their evil actions*.

I had indeed intended to examine the principal consequences that are derived from this by the more recent patrons of this **Manichaean error** <term>Manichaeism: an ancient dualistic heresy that taught a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness</term>, specifically the **Fanatics** <note>In this context, "Fanatics" refers to radical sectarian groups or Pietists who challenged established Lutheran orthodoxy</note>; but since I have been forced to extend the limits of this discussion further than I had previously anticipated, I prefer to remain silent about these matters rather than say too little.

In the meantime, I pray to God, the **Thrice Best and Greatest** <term>Optimum Maximum: a traditional honorific title for God, adapted from the Roman "Jupiter Optimus Maximus"</term>, that He might graciously deign to purge the minds of men from these impure drosses—which they must accept as stemming from the filth of the will, not of matter—with the flames of the Divine Spirit, so that the **Church of the purer parts** <note>A common self-designation for the Lutheran Church during the Reformation and post-Reformation periods</note> might find in the future the same abundant occasion it has had until now to congratulate itself on its excellent additions and to celebrate His name with deserved praises!
